# AgentBox

A Go daemon and command-line tool (`cmd/agentbox`, `internal/`) and an Electron desktop app (`desktop/`). Go and Node come from mise (`mise.toml`).

## What it is

AgentBox runs several AI coding agents against one project at the same time, each in a Linux
container of its own.

- **The daemon owns the state.** `internal/daemon` is the control plane: every agent operation goes
  through it (slow ones as jobs), and it serves the HTTP API from `internal/api` over a unix socket
  at `~/.local/share/agentbox/run/agentbox.sock`. All state is one SQLite database, `state.db`
  (`internal/state`). The CLI and the app are both clients of that socket (D15).
- **The desktop app is a thin client**: its main process only relays the socket to the renderer, with
  no AgentBox logic, Incus or git (D19). The renderer's API types are **generated from Go** into
  [`desktop/src/shared/api.ts`](desktop/src/shared/api.ts): after changing `internal/api`, run
  `UPDATE_TS=1 go test ./internal/api` or `TestTypeScriptTypesAreUpToDate` fails (D18).
- **An agent is a machine, a worktree and a branch**: an Incus container, a git worktree on
  `agentbox/<slug>` (prefix configurable, `internal/agent/branch.go`), its own network and a tmux
  terminal with its AI tool running. A project's **lead** is its chat: it runs on the host with no
  machine, directs the agents over MCP and never does the work itself.
- **Six AI tools**: Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Cursor, Gemini CLI and GitHub Copilot CLI, driven by the app's chat through **ACP**
  adapters (`internal/acp`, `ChatAdapters` in `internal/agent/chat.go`, D40).
- **Project memory** (`internal/memory`, D72): events, memories, tasks, artifacts and reports in the
  same database, searched with FTS5; no model calls or embeddings in the store. Capture from the
  daemon's chokepoints, consolidation on the tool's cheap model, and a context builder that gives
  each agent the slice its task needs.
- **Token ledger**: `token_usage`, one row per model per turn (`internal/chat/tokens.go`), read by
  `agentbox tokens` and each project's Tokens tab. Claude Code chats compact at the installation's
  compact window (500k by default); the desktop tools and Playwright belong to a `desktop` subagent,
  searches go to an `Explore` subagent on Haiku, at most three subagents at once (D83–D86).
- **The brief** is the instructions each AI tool gets about its machine, rendered by `internal/brief`
  from [`brief.md.tmpl`](internal/brief/brief.md.tmpl) (agents) and `lead.md.tmpl` (the lead), with
  the project's notes (`internal/notes`) and memory folded in. It is resent with every model call,
  so keep it short. Golden tests: `go test ./internal/brief -update` after changing a template.

## Where it runs

AgentBox runs in a VM, and the `agentbox` on the user's machine is that VM's front end
(`internal/hostvm`): `agentbox vm …` manages the VM, and every other command runs inside it.

- **Linux**: Cloud Hypervisor (`agentbox vm init`, `internal/hostvm/chv`), booting a ready-made
  disk with its packages installed (`vmdisk.go`, the `vmdisk-<version>` release the
  [Published VM disk](.github/workflows/published-vm-disk.yml) workflow makes), or Debian's cloud
  image when there's none, whose first boot installs them. Host mode (Incus on the
  machine itself) is no longer offered, but still runs for installs from earlier releases until
  `agentbox vm migrate` moves them (`MovePrompt` in `desktop/src/renderer/components/RunInVM.tsx`),
  for root, inside agents, and with `AGENTBOX_FRONT_END=host` (CI); `hostvm.Front` decides.
- **Mac** (D92): Lima, with krunkit when installed (gives memory back) and vz otherwise
  (`internal/hostvm/krunkit.go`). The socket is forwarded to its usual path, the Mac's home is shared
  at the same path, and worktrees go there (`AGENTBOX_WORKTREES`). Android is off.
  `AGENTBOX_FRONT_END=vm AGENTBOX_VM_TYPE=qemu` tests the front end on Linux.

- **Windows** (D94): `agentbox.exe` (`cmd/agentbox/main_windows.go`, `internal/hostwsl`) runs
  everything in a WSL 2 distro of AgentBox's own, and relays the apps to its daemon over a named
  pipe. `agentbox wsl install` installs WSL itself behind Windows' administrator prompt (exit
  status 3: Windows has to restart), `agentbox wsl init` makes the distro; both apps' Setup run them.
- **Installing** is one line per system, both scripts in `internal/installsh` (tested against fake
  machines, published by `scripts/r2-publish.sh` with each stable release): `install.sh` on Linux
  and a Mac, `install.ps1` on Windows.
- **The native app** (`native/`, Rust and GPUI, experimental) is a second client of the socket with
  the `agentbox` tool built in (`scripts/native-cli.sh`), packaged by `scripts/native-package.sh`:
  nightlies for Linux, Mac and Windows, releases for Windows, whose installer is
  `native/packaging/windows/installer.nsi` (NSIS, per user). It sets the machine up itself where
  there is none (`native/crates/app/src/app/machine_setup.rs`).

## Conventions

- **The app's text is translated** (`desktop/src/shared/i18n`): every user-visible string in the
  desktop app is a key in `en-US.ts` and `pt-BR.ts`, shown with `useT()`/`t()` from
  `renderer/lib/i18n.tsx`; `i18n.test.ts` and the typecheck fail when pt-BR lacks a key. A language
  is a catalog file plus a line in `languages.ts`. The CLI, the brief and the chats stay in English.
- **The look is one set of tokens for both apps**:
  [`desktop/src/shared/design-tokens.json`](desktop/src/shared/design-tokens.json) holds the colours
  (dark and light), type scale, spacing, radii and elevation. `node desktop/scripts/tokens.mjs`
  writes `desktop/src/renderer/tokens.css` and `native/crates/app/src/theme/tokens.rs` from it;
  a test in each app fails when they are stale. Don't write a colour, a `text-[Npx]` or a shadow
  recipe in a component: ask for a role (`styles.css` says what each is for). Panels are flat with
  a hairline, regions are separated by `border-line-faint`, labels are sentence case, and only
  menus (`shadow-pop`) and dialogs (`shadow-modal`) cast a shadow.
- **Migrations are appended, never edited**: `migrations` in
  [`internal/state/state.go`](internal/state/state.go), tracked with `PRAGMA user_version`.
- **Decisions and features are explained in their pull request**: context, what was decided and
  rejected, what was checked, where the code is, what it still can't do. The code cites decisions by
  number (D1–D95); their records aren't in this repository.
- **[`CHANGELOG.md`](CHANGELOG.md) is generated** by release-please (D95) from conventional-commit PR
  titles, so a PR's title is its changelog line: write it for a user. `feat:` is Added, `fix:`/`perf:`
  Fixed, `refactor:` Changed; `test:`, `ci:`, `docs:` and `chore:` don't appear.

## Build and test

```bash
go test ./internal/cli ./internal/brief   # the packages you changed
go build -o bin/agentbox ./cmd/agentbox   # "agentbox version dev"; bin/ is gitignored
npm --prefix desktop start                # build and launch the app unpacked, in seconds
npm --prefix desktop run dist             # installers in desktop/dist/: minutes, only when packaging changed
```

Run only the tests your change touches: `go test` on the packages you changed (and on those that use
an exported API you changed), and for the app the test files of what you changed (`cd desktop && node
--test src/…/x.test.ts`), plus `typecheck` and `lint`. Don't run `go test ./...` or a bare
`npm --prefix desktop test`: CI runs the whole suite, and on an agent's VM it takes every other agent's
memory. Run it only when your task, or a message from the lead or the user, asks for it by name. The slow
packages (`internal/daemon`, `internal/chat`, `internal/agent`) run tests in parallel, and
`internal/state`/`internal/memory` migrate a template database once per binary.

[CI](.github/workflows/ci.yml) is billed by the minute (the repository is private; macOS 10x,
Windows 2x), so a run runs only what its files can break. A first job checks the PR title as a
conventional commit (`feat|fix|refactor|docs|chore|test|perf|ci`) and works out, with
[`scripts/ci-changes.sh`](scripts/ci-changes.sh), what the change touches; the other jobs skip.
Go is anything but `desktop/`, `mobile/`, `docs/`, `promo/`, `packaging/`, `scripts/`, `.github/` and
root prose, plus `desktop/src/shared/api.ts`, `scripts/check-coverage.sh` and
`.github/coverage-floor.txt`: a file Go embeds or a test reads belongs under a package (or in that
list). The desktop app is `desktop/` and `vnc.js`; the phone app is `mobile/` and the desktop's
`shared/api.ts` and `shared/i18n/`. A change to `ci.yml` or `ci-changes.sh` runs everything, macOS
and Windows included. A new push cancels the run it supersedes.

- **Go tests and coverage**: `scripts/check-coverage.sh`, the one `go test ./...`, with a floor in
  [`.github/coverage-floor.txt`](.github/coverage-floor.txt), bumped as coverage rises, never
  lowered. It includes `TestTypeScriptTypesAreUpToDate`. Packages a change doesn't reach come from
  the test cache, coverage included: CI sets each file's mtime from its git object id, since a
  test that opens a file is cached by that file's mtime and size.
- **Go vet, lint, tidy**: `go mod tidy` with no diff, `go vet ./...` (and with `-tags integration`:
  Incus tests are only vetted, D49), `golangci-lint` (`.golangci.yml`), every package vetted for
  darwin, and builds for darwin/arm64, linux/arm64 and Windows.
- **Desktop**: `npm --prefix desktop` `lint` (oxlint, [`desktop/.oxlintrc.json`](desktop/.oxlintrc.json),
  used because typescript-eslint doesn't support TypeScript 7; only `react-hooks`' two rules from its
  React plugin), `typecheck`, `test` (Node's test runner, with coverage), `build`, and the committed
  `vnc.js` matching its build.
- **macOS** (cgo, signed, the vz driver) and **Windows** (the WSL front end): on pushes to `main`,
  and on a PR labelled `ci:full` (adding the label runs just these two, whatever changed), when the
  change reaches what they test: `go.mod`/`go.sum`, `mise.toml`, `cmd/`, a package their tests
  import (`go list -deps -test` of `internal/hostvm/...`, `internal/paths`, `internal/api` and `internal/iossim` for
  darwin; `internal/hostos` and `internal/hostwsl/...` for Windows), a file only that OS builds,
  and for macOS `scripts/mac-sign.sh` and the entitlements.
- **The native app on Windows** (`native-windows`): a release build and the installer, installed
  and uninstalled on the runner, on pushes to `main` and on a PR labelled `ci:full`, when the change
  reaches `native/` or `scripts/native-(package|cli).sh`. Linux type-checks it for Windows on every
  native change. `WINDOWS_RUN=wine scripts/native-package.sh windows …` tries the packaging on Linux.
- **govulncheck**: weekly, on `main`, and on PRs that change `go.mod`/`go.sum`.

Go caches are saved by `main`'s runs only and restored by PRs, so a PR's tests skip packages it
doesn't reach. [Base image](.github/workflows/base-image.yml) runs on PRs that change
`internal/image/` (its tests aside), or by hand.

## Previewing the sidebar and the right-hand panel

Both are narrow fixed-width columns, prone to overflow: a `<pre>`, an unbroken URL, or any flex/grid
child without `min-w-0` widens them. `desktop/src/renderer/dev/preview.tsx` renders both against
fixtures built to trigger that (`dev/fixtures.ts`); it isn't part of the app build.

```bash
npm --prefix desktop run preview                                    # serve it, print the URL
npm --prefix desktop run preview -- --shots out                     # screenshot every scenario in dev/scenarios.json
npm --prefix desktop run preview -- --shots out --against HEAD~1    # and before/after against another commit
npm --prefix desktop run preview -- --shots out --lang pt-BR           # in another language; overflow is reported
npm --prefix desktop run preview -- --shots out --only window-         # only the whole app at window sizes (1920×1080, portrait, 800×600, 480)
```

`?app=project` (or `home`, `pulls`, `agent-99`, `settings`) renders the whole App, where below `lg`
the sidebar and below 1100px the right-hand panel become drawers; a page wider than its window is reported too.

A scenario is a URL (`?app=agent-99&theme=light`, see the comment atop `preview.tsx`). `--against`
checks the ref out into a throwaway worktree (refs after #82 only). It uses `/usr/bin/chromium` when
present, else `npx playwright install chromium` once.

`--shots` is for overflow and before/after checks. Proof for a PR is a recording plus `agentbox media
screenshot` of the preview in the agent's display, made by the desktop subagent.

## The agents' base image

Setup downloads it (`internal/image/published.go`), adding the Codex and OpenCode tools on top when they
are on, unless Android, dev caches or Incus are (`Components.NeedsLocalBuild`), from the
`image-<version>` prerelease on this repository's GitHub releases, or first from its copy on the CDN
(`downloads.agentbox.linting.dev/images/`, `scripts/r2-images.sh`), compressed with zstd and split in
128 MiB parts that Setup downloads at once, resumes, joins and checks (`internal/image/download.go`;
`scripts/github-images.sh` publishes it, and keeps only the newest image release; app releases,
release-please and the update check never see it), and
`agentbox image build` makes it on the user's machine from Debian and
[`internal/image/provision.sh`](internal/image/provision.sh) otherwise, or when the download fails.

- **What may be published**: only what the [Published image](.github/workflows/published-image.yml)
  workflow builds on `main`, the image with no components and without `unpublished`
  (`published.go`): Claude Code, its ACP adapter (it bundles Anthropic's Agent SDK) and Cursor's
  SDK, which we may not redistribute, and which each machine installs itself. Every other tool in
  `tools.txt` must be in `toolLicenses` with a license that allows it (`TestEveryToolIsPublishedOrNot`).
  Its Debian packages are GPL and others, so the exact package list and where their sources are
  (snapshot.debian.org) go next to it, as the GPL asks. **Never publish an image built any other
  way**, such as a user's own, which has Claude Code in it.
- **Agent tools** (Go, Node, pnpm, Claude Code, gh, Codex, OpenCode, the ACP adapters, the Playwright
  MCP server) are pinned in [`tools.txt`](internal/image/tools.txt), one per line with the command
  that proves it works. **To move one on, change its line and nothing else**; don't bump
  `image.Version`. A daemon finding other tools on its base updates them in place in the background
  (`image.UpdateTools`, `internal/daemon/imagetools.go`), swapping the copy in only when every tool
  checks out (`image.UseBase`); on failure the base stays and Setup offers a rebuild.
  `internal/agent/chat.go` takes the ACP adapters' versions from the same file.
- **OpenCode 2 is the exception**: it is not in `tools.txt` nor in the image. Each agent installs its
  npm platform package at its first OpenCode 2 start (`ensureOpenCode2InAgent`,
  `internal/agent/toolaccounts.go`), pinned by `image.OpenCode2Version` and linked as `opencode2`
  (needs the network then); the host's lead installs it the first time it needs it. An installation
  chooses with `state.SettingOpenCodeVersion`; OpenCode 1 is the default.
- **Anything in `provision.sh`** means bumping `image.Version` in
  [`image.go`](internal/image/image.go), which makes Setup ask for a rebuild, as does turning an
  optional component on or off. The [Base image](.github/workflows/base-image.yml) workflow builds it
  on every PR that changes `internal/image/`.

Agents' temporary files, including `t.TempDir()`, go to a tmpfs on `/t` (`TMPDIR`), capped at 2 GiB as each
machine starts (`agent.CapTmp`, no rebuild): a unix socket's
path must stay under 107 bytes, and `/tmp` is where Incus mounts worktrees. `--dev-caches` fills the
Go, npm and Electron caches from this repository at build time. `sudo scripts/check-personalise.sh`
checks `personalise.sh` without Incus.

## Testing against a real daemon

An agent's own machine has no Incus, so image builds, devices and networking can only be unit-tested
there, against fakes. **Nesting** gives an agent a real Incus of its own:

- `agentbox image build --incus` adds Incus to the base image (`image.Components.Incus`), off by default.
- A project turns it on with `PATCH /v1/projects/<name>` (`Project.Nesting`), in the app under the
  project's Settings, "Testing AgentBox itself"; refused unless the base image has Incus.
- New agents of that project get it set up (`agent.Manager.EnsureNesting`,
  `internal/agent/nesting.go`): a `dir` storage pool and the bridge `10.88.8.1/24`, which can't clash
  with the host's 10.8.8.0/24. No `/dev/kvm`: containers only.
- Inside, `go test -tags integration ./internal/incus/...`, `sudo agentbox host setup` (idempotent),
  and `agentbox image build` then `agentbox create` work as on a real host.

## The hub

The hub, the server half (D44), is its own program in [`hub/`](hub/), in this module:
`hub/cmd/agentbox-hub` and `hub/internal/hub`, with the npm launcher `npx agentbox-hub` in
`hub/npm/` (`hub/scripts/npm-build.sh` builds it, `hub/npm/PUBLISHING.md` publishes it). It was
lintingdotdev/agentbox-hub until #547 brought it back. The two halves share only
[`hubapi/`](hubapi/), the protocol: the hub imports it, and nothing else of AgentBox
(`TestHubImportsOnlyHubapi`). `internal/` can't import the hub, which Go's `internal/` rule
enforces, and `hubapi/` must never import `internal/` or the rest of this module.

```bash
go test ./hub/... ./hubapi/...
go build -o bin/agentbox-hub ./hub/cmd/agentbox-hub
hub/scripts/npm-build.sh 0.0.0-dev     # the npm packages, in hub/npm/dist/
```

CI runs the hub's Go tests with everyone else's; a change to `hub/`, `hubapi/` or `go.mod` also
builds its npm packages and runs `npx agentbox-hub --version` from them (the Hub job).

## Commits

Conventional commits: `feat: ...`, `fix: ...`, `refactor: ...`, `docs: ...`, and `chore(release): <version>` for a release.

## Releasing

Releasing is merging release-please's PR (D95, `.github/workflows/release.yml`, configured in
`.github/release-please-config.json` and `.release-please-manifest.json`). It keeps one open release
PR that bumps `version` in `desktop/package.json` and `desktop/package-lock.json` and rewrites
`CHANGELOG.md`, minor if any `feat:` landed, patch otherwise.

1. Land the changes on `main`, each PR titled for a user.
2. Find the release PR (`gh pr list --search "head:release-please--branches--main"`) and fix any
   `CHANGELOG.md` line that reads like a commit message.

# Troubleshooting AgentBox's setup

Setup sent you a check of `agentbox doctor` that failed, with what it found, its suggested fix
and the end of the daemon's log. Find out why it fails, fix what you can, and say plainly what's
left for the user.

## Where you are

You run where the AgentBox daemon runs. On Linux and macOS that is AgentBox's VM, not the user's
own machine: the user's home directory is shared with it at the same path, but their desktop,
their BIOS, their groups and their package manager are out of your reach. On a machine from
before the VM (host mode) or under WSL you are on that machine itself, without root unless
`sudo -n true` works.

## What you can do from here

- `agentbox doctor` (add `--json` to read it exactly) runs every check again; `agentbox doctor
  --fix` retries what fixes itself: the base image download, the chat's AI tool and the GitHub
  CLI. Run it before anything else, and again at the end to show the fix worked.
- Read the daemon's log: `~/.local/share/agentbox/daemon.log` (`tail -n 200`, `grep -i error`).
- Look at the disks (`df -h`, `du -sh ~/.local/share/agentbox/*`), the network (`curl -sSI
  https://downloads.agentbox.linting.dev/images`, `curl -sSI https://api.github.com`), DNS,
  proxies (`env | grep -i proxy`).
- Incus: `incus info`, `incus storage list`, `incus image list`, `systemctl status incus`.
- `agentbox image build` makes the base image; `agentbox jobs` follows it.
- Ask before removing anything of the user's (agents, worktrees, images, files) to free space.

## What only the user can do

Give these as commands or steps for them to run on their own machine, and say why. Never claim
you ran them.

- Turning on virtualization (Intel VT-x or AMD-V, "SVM") in the BIOS or UEFI settings.
- Joining the `kvm` group (`sudo usermod -aG kvm "$USER"`, then logging out and back in), or
  `sudo agentbox host setup`, which does it and the rest of host setup.
- Installing Lima on a Mac (`brew install lima`), or updating macOS.
- `agentbox vm start`, `agentbox vm stop` and `agentbox vm init` on their machine, for a VM that
  is stopped, stuck or was never made.
- Logging in: `agentbox auth claude` (or `codex`, `opencode`, `cursor`) and `agentbox auth github`
  open a browser, and only the user can approve them.
- Freeing space on their own disk outside AgentBox's folders.

## How to answer

Say in a sentence what was wrong, what you changed, and what the user has to run, if anything, in
a code block each. If you can't tell why it fails, say what you checked and what you'd look at
next; don't guess a fix.

AgentBox

A team of AI coding agents on your own computer, each with a Linux machine of its own, directed by a lead you chat with.

Download · Quick start · How it compares · Docs

Tell a project's **lead** what you want. It starts the agents the work needs, each one Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Cursor, Gemini CLI or GitHub Copilot CLI on **a Linux machine of its own**: its own branch and worktree, Docker, ports and databases, and a desktop with a browser that you can watch live and take over. Agents test their work in the real app and keep screenshots and recordings as proof, so you review what they built, not their word for it, and merge from the same window. The lead answers their questions, passes on the ones only you can answer, and remembers what the project has learned for the next agent. It all runs on your computer, and it's MIT-licensed. ## Why AgentBox - **A real machine per agent, not just a worktree.** Each agent gets a Linux container with its own network, Docker and every port free, so ten agents can run the same dev server and database at once without colliding. Snapshot one, fork a new agent from it, or pause it with its memory intact. - **A desktop and browser for every agent.** Agents click through the app they're changing with a real mouse and keyboard. Open an agent's **Desktop** to watch it, and click **Take control** to drive it yourself. - **A lead that directs the agents.** The project's chat creates agents, briefs them, answers their questions, sends you the ones that need you, and tells you when the work is ready. You talk to one chat, not ten terminals. - **Proof you can review.** Every agent's work comes with its recording, chapter by chapter, its screenshots and test reports, the diff, its pull request and CI, and a timeline of what it did. Merge or request changes from the review. - **Project memory.** What one agent learns (a flaky test, a decision, a setup gotcha) is kept for the project, and every new agent starts briefed on it. - **On your phone.** Pair a phone with a QR code to follow the lead and the agents live, answer their questions and merge ([docs/phone.md](docs/phone.md)). - **Six AI tools, your own accounts.** Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Cursor, Gemini CLI and GitHub Copilot CLI in the same chat, with tool calls, diffs, plans and subagents in one timeline. Use several Claude and GitHub accounts, and see what each agent spent in tokens. - **Local and open.** Agents run in a VM on your own computer, with the CPUs and memory you give it, so your code stays with you. No account with us, and MIT-licensed.
Review: an agent's proof, diff and pull request, then Merge Timeline: what an agent did, step by step
Work: everything your agents did, live and past, across projects
## How it compares Each of these runs coding agents in parallel; they differ in what an agent gets, and in who directs it. On Linux and on a Mac: ```bash curl -fsSL https://downloads.agentbox.linting.dev/install.sh | sh ``` On Windows, in PowerShell: ```powershell irm https://downloads.agentbox.linting.dev/install.ps1 | iex ``` On Linux it installs the `.deb` on Debian and Ubuntu, the `.pacman` on Arch, and the AppImage anywhere else; on a Mac, AgentBox in Applications; on Windows, the installer, for your user alone. The app's **Setup** walks you through the rest the first time it runs. # AgentBox desktop app

A client of the AgentBox daemon: projects and agents, with each agent's chat, terminal, browser, Android emulator, media and snapshots, and a Setup page for the machine.

## Run

```bash
npm install
npm start          # builds into out/ and opens the app
```

The app uses the same socket as the CLI: `~/.local/share/agentbox/run/agentbox.sock`, or `AGENTBOX_SOCKET`. When no daemon answers, the app starts one with `agentbox daemon start`, so put `agentbox` on your `PATH` or set `AGENTBOX_BIN`.

## Package

```bash
npm run dist       # dist/AgentBox-<version>-x86_64.AppImage
```

`dist` builds `../bin/agentbox` for the app's version, builds the app, and packages both with electron-builder. The packaged app:
- keeps its own copy of `agentbox` in `~/.local/share/agentbox/bin`, and starts the daemon from it;
- links `~/.local/bin/agentbox` to that copy from the Setup page (**Install command-line tool**);
- restarts a daemon of another version, or one that started without the `incus-admin` or `kvm` group, when no job is running (D27, D28).

On a Mac, `npm run dist -- --mac` packages `dist/AgentBox-<version>-mac-<arch>.dmg` and `.zip` instead
(`--arm64`, `--x64` or both; default this Mac's). The Mac app carries two binaries: `bin/agentbox`, the
macOS front end of AgentBox's Linux VM, and `bin/agentbox-linux`, the Linux build it installs in that
VM (D92). The app keeps both beside each other in
`~/.local/share/agentbox/bin`, and until the VM exists its first screen sets it up.

A new machine's setup is in the README's [Install](../README.md#install), and a Mac's in [macOS and Windows](../docs/install.md#macos-and-windows-alpha).

## Develop

```bash
npm run typecheck
npm run build
UPDATE_TS=1 go test ./internal/api   # from the repository root, after changing internal/api/types.go
```

- `src/main`: the Electron main process. It relays API calls, the event stream, WebSocket streams and media files to the daemon's unix socket, and installs the command-line tool. It holds no AgentBox logic.
- `src/preload`: the bridge the renderer gets.
- `src/renderer`: the React UI (Tailwind, Radix, xterm.js, noVNC). The chat is `components/chat/`, with `lib/chat.ts` keeping each agent's thread up to date from the event stream (react-markdown, Shiki and jsdiff).
- `src/shared/api.ts`: the API types, generated from `internal/api/types.go`.
- `build/icon.svg`: the app icon; `build/icon.png` is rendered from it with `rsvg-convert -w 512 -h 512`.

The demo scripts in [`scripts/demo/`](../scripts/demo/) drive the app end to end with Playwright, on a private X display: `step-6.mjs` (agents and terminals), `step-7.mjs` (browser), `step-8.mjs` (media), `step-9.mjs` (Android), `chat.mjs` (the chat) and `packaging.mjs` (the AppImage).

# AgentBox documentation

AgentBox runs several AI coding agents against one project at the same time, each in a Linux
container of its own so they can't collide. It is a Go daemon and command-line tool
(`cmd/agentbox`, `internal/`) plus an Electron desktop app (`desktop/`).

## The shape of it

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph host["Your machine"]
        CLI["CLI (cmd/agentbox)"]
        App["Desktop app (desktop/)"]
        Daemon["Daemon (internal/daemon)"]
        DB[("state.db\ninternal/state")]
        CLI -- "unix socket" --> Daemon
        App -- "unix socket, via main process" --> Daemon
        Daemon --> DB
    end
    subgraph containers["One Incus container per agent"]
        Agent1["agent-01\nworktree + branch + tmux + AI tool"]
        Agent2["agent-02\nworktree + branch + tmux + AI tool"]
    end
    Daemon -- "incus, ssh-less exec" --> Agent1
    Daemon -- "incus, ssh-less exec" --> Agent2
    Daemon -. "optional tunnel" .-> Hub[("A hub\n(hubapi/)")]
```

- **The daemon owns the state.** [`internal/daemon`](../internal/daemon) is the control plane:
  every agent operation goes through it, the slow ones as jobs, and it serves the HTTP API from
  [`internal/api`](../internal/api) over a unix socket at
  `~/.local/share/agentbox/run/agentbox.sock`. All state lives in one SQLite database, `state.db`,
  in [`internal/state`](../internal/state). The CLI is a client of that socket, and so is the
  desktop app.
- **The desktop app is a thin client.** Its main process only relays the socket to the renderer:
  no AgentBox logic, no Incus, no git. The API types the renderer uses are generated from Go into
  [`desktop/src/shared/api.ts`](../desktop/src/shared/api.ts).
- **An agent is a machine, a worktree and a branch.** `agentbox create` gives it an Incus
  container, a git worktree on a branch named after its work, like `agentbox/fix-login-redirect` (the prefix is a project setting), its own network and a tmux terminal with its AI
  tool already running.
- **A project also has a lead** — its chat — which runs on the host with no machine of its own, so
  a project nobody has chatted with costs nothing. It directs the project's agents over MCP tools
  and never does the work itself.
- **Three AI tools:** Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode, all driven through ACP (Agent Client
  Protocol) adapters.
- **Project memory is what the project knows, kept across agents:** events, memories, tasks,
  artifacts and reports, searched with SQLite FTS5.
- **A hub is optional.** It's a separate server program, `npx agentbox-hub`, in [`hub/`](../hub),
  which shares only the protocol, [`hubapi/`](../hubapi), with the rest.

# AgentBox hub

The hub: accounts, the environments (machines running AgentBox) that connect to
it, and the proxy that reaches them. It is the server half of AgentBox, a
program of its own in AgentBox's module; everything that *uses* a hub is in the
rest of this repository. MIT, like the rest.

```bash
npx agentbox-hub                     # or, from the repository's root:
go test ./hub/... ./hubapi/...
go build -o bin/agentbox-hub ./hub/cmd/agentbox-hub
bin/agentbox-hub                     # SQLite in AgentBox's data directory, on 127.0.0.1:8080
```

The first start prints a one-time setup link and its QR code: whoever opens it
first becomes the hub's owner. Everything else that connects — the app, the
CLI, a browser, a phone, an environment — asks with `POST /v1/pair`, shows a
code, and is let in when a device already connected approves it
(`internal/hub/pairing.go`, the hub's own pages in `pages.html`). There are no
passwords, except on accounts made before pairing, which keep theirs.
`agentbox-hub link` prints another setup link, or, once the hub has an owner,
a 15-minute sign-in link for them.

Using a hub, and running one on a server (`--listen`, `--url`, Postgres with
`--db`, a TLS proxy in front): [`docs/hub.md`](../docs/hub.md).
Publishing the npm package: [`npm/PUBLISHING.md`](npm/PUBLISHING.md).

## Stable addresses for phones

An environment's phones can reach it from anywhere through a Cloudflare
Tunnel. With a Cloudflare zone, the hub gives each environment one that
stays the same: the first time the environment asks
(`POST /v1/environment/tunnel`, with its environment token), the hub makes a
remotely-managed tunnel named `agentbox-<id>` and a proxied CNAME
`<id>.<zone>` → `<tunnel>.cfargotunnel.com`, routes it to the daemon
(`hubapi.EnvironmentTunnelOrigin`), and answers the hostname and the tunnel's
token; after that it answers the same hostname every time
(`internal/hub/tunnels.go`, `cloudflare.go`). The environment runs
cloudflared with the token: phone traffic goes through Cloudflare straight to
it, never through the hub, and phones still pair with the environment's own
one-time secret, which the hub never sees.

To turn it on, give the hub:

- **A zone**, by its ID (the zone's Overview page in Cloudflare's dashboard):
  `--cloudflare-zone <id>` or `AGENTBOX_HUB_CLOUDFLARE_ZONE`. Hostnames are
  one level below the zone, which Cloudflare's Universal SSL covers.
- **An API token**, in `AGENTBOX_HUB_CLOUDFLARE_TOKEN`, or a file named by
  `AGENTBOX_HUB_CLOUDFLARE_TOKEN_FILE` (a mounted secret, say); never a flag.
  Make it under My Profile → API Tokens → Create Custom Token, with:
  - Account › **Cloudflare Tunnel** › Edit, on the zone's account;
  - Zone › **DNS** › Edit, and Zone › **Zone** › Read, on the zone.

Without both, the hub answers 501 and environments use a quick tunnel. Once an
hour it removes the tunnels and records of deleted environments, and of those
neither connected nor asking for 60 days; one that comes back gets its
hostname again.

## Tailscale instead of Cloudflare

`--transport tailscale` (or `AGENTBOX_HUB_TRANSPORT=tailscale`) puts each
environment in your tailnet instead of giving it a Cloudflare Tunnel: asked
the same `POST /v1/environment/tunnel`, the hub answers an auth key
(`hubapi.TransportTailscale`), the environment's daemon joins the tailnet
with it as a node named `agentbox-<name>-<id>` (tailscaled in userspace mode,
next to the daemon), serves on it with `tailscale serve`, and reports the
address it got (`POST /v1/environment/address`), which the hub lists on the
environment. Only the tailnet's devices reach it; nothing is on the internet,
and the hub sees none of the traffic (`internal/hub/tailscale.go`,
`tunnels.go`).

Give the hub one of:

- **An auth key**, in `AGENTBOX_HUB_TAILSCALE_AUTHKEY` or a file named by
  `AGENTBOX_HUB_TAILSCALE_AUTHKEY_FILE`: reusable, pre-approved, and tagged
  `tag:agentbox` (the admin console's Settings → Keys). Every environment
  gets the same key, and the hub can't remove their nodes.
- **An OAuth client**, `--tailscale-oauth-client <id>` or
  `AGENTBOX_HUB_TAILSCALE_OAUTH_CLIENT`, with its secret in
  `AGENTBOX_HUB_TAILSCALE_OAUTH_SECRET` or `…_SECRET_FILE`, made under
  Settings → OAuth clients with the **Auth Keys** (write) and **Devices
  Core** (write) scopes and the tag `tag:agentbox`. The hub makes each
  environment a one-off key that lasts an hour, and removes its node when the
  environment is deleted or idle for 60 days.

Secrets are never flags and never logged. `--tailscale-tailnet` (or
`AGENTBOX_HUB_TAILSCALE_TAILNET`) names the tailnet, as Settings → General
shows it, `-` (the key's own) by default; `--tailscale-tag` changes the tag.
The tailnet needs MagicDNS and HTTPS certificates on, and a policy that owns
the tag and lets your devices reach it; AgentBox's
[`docs/hub.md`](../docs/hub.md#tailscale-instead-of-cloudflare)
has the policy. A hub moved from Cloudflare to Tailscale keeps its zone, when
it still has one, only to remove the tunnels it made before.

## Where it came from

The hub was `internal/hub/` and `agentbox server` in AgentBox until
[#21](https://github.com/leciric/agentbox/pull/21) split it out (commit
`6a7091e`) into its own repository, lintingdotdev/agentbox-hub, where it got
`npx agentbox-hub`, pairing and Tailscale. [#547](https://github.com/leciric/agentbox/pull/547)
brought it back as `hub/`, from that repository's `feat-tailscale` (`d2e5bd4`),
whose history stays there. It stays a separate program (D44): it shares only
`hubapi` with the rest of AgentBox.

## `hubapi`, AgentBox's protocol

The hub needs one thing from the rest of AgentBox: [`hubapi`](../hubapi/), the
wire types, the token prefixes, the endpoint paths, and the yamux settings both
ends of the tunnel configure. It imports nothing else of AgentBox: no client,
no daemon, no CLI (`TestHubImportsOnlyHubapi`). A change to `hubapi` is
checked against the hub and the client by the same `go test ./...`.

## Testing

`internal/hub/connector_test.go` is an environment for the hub's own tests;
the real connector is AgentBox's `internal/remote`. It speaks the
protocol and nothing more, so a passing test here means the hub matches
`hubapi`, not that it matches AgentBox. Checking the two against each other
means running a real AgentBox against a real hub: `scripts/demo/remote.mjs`
does, with `AGENTBOX_HUB_BIN` pointing at a built `agentbox-hub`.

The store tests run on SQLite by default, and on Postgres when
`AGENTBOX_TEST_POSTGRES` names a database they may empty.

# Native app (proof of concept)

A native desktop client for AgentBox in Rust, drawn with [GPUI](https://www.gpui.rs/) (Zed's UI
framework) and [gpui-component](https://github.com/longbridge/gpui-kit) for widgets. It lives beside
the Electron app in `desktop/`, which it doesn't replace yet.

Like the Electron app it is a thin client of the daemon (D15/D19): it asks over the daemon's unix
socket and shows what comes back, with no AgentBox logic of its own.

| crate                 | what it is                                                                   |
| --------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `crates/agentbox-api` | the API's types (generated from Go), a client for the socket, an SSE parser |
| `crates/app`          | the app, `agentbox-native`                                                   |
| `crates/fake-daemon`  | a stand-in daemon with fixture agents, for where agents can't run            |
| `crates/office`       | the Office (#668): its layout, walking, camera and a wgpu renderer, no GPUI  |

## Build and run

Rust comes from rustup (`rustup default stable`). On Linux GPUI needs the X11/Wayland and Vulkan
development packages:

```bash
sudo apt-get install libxkbcommon-x11-dev libwayland-dev libvulkan-dev libfontconfig-dev libfreetype-dev libx11-xcb-dev mesa-vulkan-drivers \
  libavformat-dev libavcodec-dev libswscale-dev libavutil-dev libclang-dev \
  libwebkit2gtk-4.1-dev libgtk-3-dev libasound2-dev
cargo run --release -p agentbox-native                       # against this machine's daemon
cargo run --release -p agentbox-native -- --socket /path.sock # or another socket (also AGENTBOX_SOCKET)
```

Without a GPU, use Mesa's software Vulkan, lavapipe:
`VK_DRIVER_FILES=/usr/share/vulkan/icd.d/lvp_icd.json`. Inside an AgentBox agent, the virtio-GPU
(Venus) device draws a black window; lavapipe works.

### Through a VM's socket forward

In VM mode the socket the app opens is forwarded into the VM, where `socat VSOCK-LISTEN:…,fork`
takes each new connection; it queues only a few at once. To try the app against that on a host
daemon, put socat in front of the socket and point the app at it:

```bash
socat UNIX-LISTEN:/t/vm.sock,fork,backlog=1 UNIX-CONNECT:$HOME/.local/share/agentbox/run/agentbox.sock &
AGENTBOX_SOCKET=/t/vm.sock cargo run -p agentbox-api --example burst -- <project> main   # how many requests never got through
AGENTBOX_SOCKET=/t/vm.sock cargo run --release -p agentbox-native
```

### Against a fake daemon

An agent's machine has no Incus, so a real daemon there has a lead but no agents.
`fake-daemon` serves a project's agents from fixtures (changing their state every few seconds, and
streaming a reply to any message) and passes everything else, the event stream included, to a real
daemon:

```bash
cargo run -p fake-daemon -- --listen /t/fake.sock --upstream ~/.local/share/agentbox/run/agentbox.sock
cargo run --release -p agentbox-native -- --socket /t/fake.sock
```

Its agents' Resources views sample made-up numbers every two seconds while the app's presence lease
asks for them (`GET /v1/presence` on the fake shows the leases it holds); the leases go on to the
upstream daemon too.

`--project` (demo), `--agents` (6), `--history` (400 messages per agent) and `--rate` (60 chunks a
second) shape the fixtures. Without `--upstream` it serves one project on its own.

`--neighbours storefront:4,quill:3` adds more projects with a few agents each (no chats), for the
Office's campus.
`--neighbours empty:0` adds one with none. `--icons demo=🦊,quill=logo.svg` gives projects icons (an
emoji, or a picture's file), which the sidebar and the Office's carpets show.

## The Office

Settings → General → Office (off by default) adds the Office to the sidebar: #668's campus of
projects' rooms, where you walk to an agent and open its chat at its desk.
`AGENTBOX_NATIVE_OFFICE=1` opens it at start.

## Cockpit mode

Settings → Experimental → Interface → Cockpit mode (the daemon's `cockpitMode`, off by default) adds a
Cockpit mode button to the top bar: every project's lead in one feed beside a live wall of agents, and
one project's agent on a stage (`crates/app/src/app/cockpit.rs`, as the Electron app's
`components/cockpit`). Esc or the button again leaves it. `AGENTBOX_NATIVE_COCKPIT=1` opens it at
start, `=<project>` or `=<project>/<agent>` focused there; the fake daemon's `--cockpit` turns the
setting on, and its `--neighbours` give their leads a short conversation each:

```bash
cargo run -p fake-daemon -- --listen /t/fake.sock --neighbours storefront:4,quill:3 --cockpit
AGENTBOX_NATIVE_SIZE=3440x1440 AGENTBOX_NATIVE_COCKPIT=demo cargo run --release -p agentbox-native -- --socket /t/fake.sock
```

- `crates/office` has no GPUI: the layout, the model, walking and the camera ported from #668's
  TypeScript (with its tests), the rooms, props and robots built in code as #668 builds them, and
  Kenney's models (`assets/kenney`, CC0). It draws with wgpu (the version GPUI uses) offscreen, on a
  thread of its own, and reads each frame back as BGRA. The app (`src/office.rs`) paints the frame
  as an image and puts the name tags, cards and chat over it in GPUI.
- It draws only while something moves or changes: still, it costs no frames and no CPU.
- On a software adapter (lavapipe, llvmpipe, WARP) it draws anyway and says so, with how to fix it.

Measured on lavapipe (no GPU, 3 cores), 1440×813, `AGENTBOX_NATIVE_BENCH=1`: walking about 28
fps (render and readback p50 29 ms), standing still 0 frames and about 1% CPU (the app's own idle).
`cargo run --release -p agentbox-office --example spike` (`OFFICE_SPIKE_BENCH=5`) is the first
spike: one Kenney model, 59 fps painted by GPUI on lavapipe.

- Frames are paced to the display (`Pace` in `engine.rs`): each is drawn for a display refresh, the
  sim steps to exactly that moment, and the view holds it until then; one frame is drawn ahead while
  GPUI shows the last. The bench's `judder` is how far a frame's step in sim time is from its step
  on screen (0 is smooth), `late` how far from its refresh it was painted.
- Depth is reversed (near 1, far 0) so floors stacked a millimetre apart don't fight from the campus
  view; pictures have mips and anisotropic filtering, Kenney's colormap stays nearest.
  `cargo run --release -p agentbox-office --example flicker` counts the pixels that flicker as the
  camera moves 1 mm at a time and writes where, in red.
- A GPU draws with 4× MSAA, a software adapter without; `AGENTBOX_OFFICE_MSAA=1` or `4` says otherwise.

## The API's types

`crates/agentbox-api/src/types.rs` is generated from `internal/api` by the same test that writes
the desktop's `api.ts`, from the same list of types:

```bash
UPDATE_TS=1 go test ./internal/api   # writes desktop/src/shared/api.ts and native/…/types.rs
```

`TestRustTypesAreUpToDate` fails when it's stale, as `TestTypeScriptTypesAreUpToDate` does. Every
struct reads Go's JSON leniently: a missing field is its zero value, null is an empty slice or map,
pointers are `Option`, and unknown fields are ignored, so an older app reads a newer daemon.

## Measuring

`AGENTBOX_NATIVE_BENCH=1` prints when the first frame and the data went out, and percentiles of the
time between frames while a chat streams. `AGENTBOX_NATIVE_OPEN=agent-02` opens that agent's chat
at start, and `AGENTBOX_NATIVE_SCROLL_BENCH=3` scrolls it 24 px a frame for 600 frames, three
seconds in, and prints the frame intervals.
`AGENTBOX_NATIVE_VIEW=work AGENTBOX_NATIVE_WORK_BENCH=500` opens the Work page, prints when its
first page arrived (`work-loaded`) and its first rows were drawn (`work-rows`), loads 500 pieces of
work and scrolls through them the same way.

# AgentBox as an AUR binary package

A PKGBUILD that installs `agentbox-bin`, a real AUR submission: it downloads the
`AgentBox-<version>-x86_64.AppImage` and `agentbox-<version>-linux-amd64` assets from a
release at [downloads.agentbox.linting.dev](https://downloads.agentbox.linting.dev/index.html) and checks them against the
release's own `SHA256SUMS`, instead of building from source like [`../aur`](../aur).

## Build and install

```bash
cd packaging/aur-bin
makepkg -si
```

The AppImage is extracted with `--appimage-extract` (no FUSE needed) and repackaged the same way
[`../aur`](../aur)'s PKGBUILD lays out a from-source build: the command-line tool at
`/usr/bin/agentbox`, the app at `/usr/lib/agentbox-desktop/`, and `/usr/bin/agentbox-desktop` as its
launcher, so the two packages conflict and provide `agentbox` for each other.

## Updating for a new release

`pkgver`'s two download sums (the AppImage and the CLI binary) are release
build artifacts and can't be known before a release is published. After tagging and publishing a
release:

```bash
packaging/aur-bin/update-checksums.sh [version]   # defaults to PKGBUILD's own pkgver
```

This fetches the release's `SHA256SUMS`, fills in `PKGBUILD`'s `sha256sums`, bumps `pkgver` and
resets `pkgrel=1`, then regenerates `.SRCINFO` with `makepkg --printsrcinfo` if `makepkg` is
available. `updpkgsums` (from Arch's `pacman-contrib`) is the usual alternative — it downloads and
hashes the files itself instead of trusting the published `SHA256SUMS`, which is a stronger check
but needs `makepkg` (and so an Arch machine) to run at all.

For a fix release that only bumps `pkgrel` (no new upstream version), edit `pkgrel` by hand and
regenerate `.SRCINFO`.

## Checking it

`namcap PKGBUILD` and, after a build, `namcap agentbox-bin-*.pkg.tar.zst` want an Arch machine; this
repository's own checks (`go test ./...`, CI) don't run either, since nothing here is Arch. Do both
before submitting a checksum update.

Same layout as [`../aur`](../aur#what-it-installs).

# AgentBox as an Arch package

A PKGBUILD that installs this checkout as the `agentbox` package, without the
AppImage. It builds the command-line tool and the desktop app here, and packages
both, with the app's own Electron (Electron 44), since Arch's `electron` is
older and the app doesn't use it.

## Build and install

```bash
cd packaging/aur
makepkg -si
```

`makepkg` builds from the working tree, so commit or stash what you want in the
package: only what is on disk is copied, but the build does not touch your tree
(everything happens in `src/`).

The build takes a few minutes the first time: `mise install` fetches the Go and
Node versions `mise.toml` pins, `npm ci` fetches the app's dependencies, and
electron-builder downloads Electron 44.

## What it installs

| Path | What |
|---|---|
| `/usr/bin/agentbox` | The command-line tool and daemon |
| `/usr/lib/agentbox-desktop/` | The desktop app, with its own Electron |
| `/usr/bin/agentbox-desktop` | Launcher: runs the app with `AGENTBOX_BIN=/usr/bin/agentbox` |
| `/usr/share/applications/agentbox-desktop.desktop` | Menu entry |
| `/usr/share/icons/hicolor/…` | Icon |

`AGENTBOX_BIN` is what makes the app use the packaged command-line tool instead
of copying its own into `~/.local/share/agentbox/bin` and asking Setup to link
it. The app and the terminal always run the same version.

Setting up a machine afterwards (Incus, groups, the base image) is the same as
the AppImage: open Setup in the app, or follow the root
[README](../../README.md#install).

## Updating

`pkgver` must match `version` in `desktop/package.json`; the build refuses to
run when they differ. On a release, bump both, set `pkgrel=1`, and rebuild.

## Limitations

- **Arch, x86_64, only.** Like the released AppImage.
- **Not reproducible in the AUR's sense.** It builds the working tree rather
  than a release tarball with checksums, so it is for local use, not for
  publishing as-is. [`packaging/aur-bin/`](../aur-bin/) is the one that
  downloads a release's assets and checksums them, and is what's actually

# AgentBox's Cloud Hypervisor, and the Linux VM's GPU

The Cloud Hypervisor every Linux VM runs: upstream's v53.0 with Spectrum OS's virtio-gpu patchset
rebased onto it ([`patches/`](patches/README.md)), and beside it crosvm's GPU device and
virglrenderer, which give the VM the host's GPU when "GPU for agents" is on
(`internal/hostvm/chv/gpu.go`). `build.sh` makes the tarball, the Cloud Hypervisor workflow
(`.github/workflows/chv.yml`) builds and publishes it as the release
`chv-<version>-<hash of its inputs>` (`publish.sh`) and pins it in `internal/hostvm/chv/tools.go` (`chvBundle`, through a pull request `pin.sh` makes)
downloads it by its SHA256: nobody compiles anything. `try.sh`, from the spike that started it
(#427), boots a throwaway guest with the tarball on a machine with KVM and a GPU and says what
the guest got.

## The pieces

```
guest: Mesa virgl (OpenGL), Mesa Venus (Vulkan)
   │  virtio-gpu (3D, blob resources, host-visible memory)
cloud-hypervisor + Spectrum's GPU patchset    ← the VMM: a vhost-user front end for virtio-gpu
   │  vhost-user, plus a shared-memory region for blobs
crosvm device gpu                             ← the device, a separate host process
   │  rutabaga
virglrenderer (GL contexts; Venus contexts in virgl_render_server)
   │
host Mesa / GPU driver on /dev/dri/renderD128
```

- **Cloud Hypervisor** has no GPU device of its own. [Spectrum OS](https://spectrum-os.org/software/cloud-hypervisor/)
  keeps a patchset adding one: `--gpu socket=…`, a vhost-user frontend for crosvm's GPU backend
  (not QEMU's `vhost-user-gpu` protocol), with patches to rust-vmm's `vhost` crates for the shared
  memory region that host-visible blobs (and so Venus) need. Their newest, `50.0-spectrum0`,
  targets Cloud Hypervisor v50.0; [`patches/`](patches/README.md) has it rebased onto v53.0, and
  says how, and what the next version costs. Without `--gpu` none of it runs: the binary takes
  AgentBox's VM's command line exactly as upstream's v53.0 does (`test/chv_args_test.sh`).
- **crosvm's `device gpu`** is crosvm's virtio-gpu device as a standalone vhost-user backend. It
  has no releases; the commit is the one Spectrum tested the patchset with.
- **virglrenderer** turns the guest's virgl (OpenGL) and Venus (Vulkan) command streams into host
  GL and Vulkan calls. Built with Venus and its render server (`libexec/virgl_render_server`,
  which crosvm starts for Venus contexts).

## build.sh

```bash
scripts/chv-gpu/build.sh [OUTPUT_DIR]     # default scripts/chv-gpu/out/
```

Builds in Docker (BuildKit), linux/amd64 only, in about 15 minutes on 4 cores.
`CARGO_BUILD_JOBS` (default 4) bounds the Rust builds: Cloud Hypervisor links with LTO. Out come
`chv-53.0-<hash>-x86_64.tar.gz`, its `.sha256`, `VERSIONS` and `HOST-LIBRARIES`, where `<hash>` is
`inputs-hash.sh`'s, of every file the build reads. Change any, and main's next run publishes a new
release, since a published build is never replaced, and opens a pull request pinning it (crosvm
doesn't build byte for byte alike twice, so the pin follows what's published, not a local build).

```
bin/cloud-hypervisor, bin/ch-remote   static; says v53.0.0-agentbox-<hash>
bin/crosvm                            glibc ≥ 2.36, RUNPATH $ORIGIN/../lib
libexec/virgl_render_server
lib/libvirglrenderer.so.1             bundled: distributions' builds often lack Venus
licenses/, VERSIONS, HOST-LIBRARIES, SHA256SUMS
```

**What the host must provide** (`HOST-LIBRARIES` lists the exact sonames): glibc 2.36 or newer
(Debian 12, Ubuntu 22.10, Fedora 37 and later), and the graphics stack it renders with:
`libepoxy`, `libdrm`, `libgbm`, `libvulkan` (the loader), `libEGL`/`libGL` through libepoxy,
`libwayland-client`, `libX11`, `libcap`. These aren't bundled on purpose: they must be the host's
own, matching its Mesa and its GPU driver. Any desktop Linux with Mesa installed has them.

Git sources go through [`fetch-git.sh`](fetch-git.sh): five tries per URL, 2 to 16 seconds
apart, since chromium.googlesource.com answers 503 now and then, and then Google's GitHub mirrors
of crosvm and minijail. Whichever serves it, the commit must be the pinned one.

Reproducibility: every source is pinned by commit or SHA-256, Debian's packages by snapshot date,
the Rust images by digest; paths are remapped, file times set to `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH`, and the
tarball written in a fixed order with fixed owners. A build and a `DOCKER_BUILD_FLAGS=--no-cache`
rebuild on one machine gave the same tarball, byte for byte, but that doesn't hold across machines:
CI's crosvm and its cloud-hypervisor binary both hashed differently from an agent's build of the
same inputs. So the claim is only same-machine, and the pin follows what CI published.

**arm64** isn't built. It would build the same way on an arm64 host (with
`aarch64-unknown-linux-musl`), but cross-building crosvm and virglrenderer needs an arm64 sysroot
of the graphics libraries, and AgentBox's Linux VM is amd64-only today anyway.

## try.sh

```bash
scripts/chv-gpu/try.sh --check            # prerequisites only
scripts/chv-gpu/try.sh                    # the run: 5 to 15 minutes, mostly apt in the guest
scripts/chv-gpu/try.sh --keep             # and keep the serial log, disk and process logs
```

Runs as your user: no root, no tap device, no firewall rules. It needs `/dev/kvm` and the render
node readable and writable by you (the `kvm` and `render` groups), `curl`, `tar`, `xz`, and one
of `cloud-localds`, `genisoimage`, `mkisofs`, `xorriso` or `mkfs.vfat`+`mcopy` for the cloud-init
seed. It then:

1. checks those, and reports the render node's driver and PCI id, the host's Mesa and
   virglrenderer packages, and its own Vulkan device;
2. starts passt (the guest's network, as in AgentBox's VM), crosvm's GPU device on the render node
   with GL (virgl) and Vulkan (Venus) contexts and no window (crosvm's stub display), and Cloud
   Hypervisor with `--gpu`, a copy of Debian 13's generic image (its kernel has `virtio_gpu`; the
   cloud kernel AgentBox's VM uses doesn't) and a cloud-init seed;
3. in the guest, cloud-init installs Mesa's drivers, `mesa-utils`, `vulkan-tools`, glmark2, vkmark
   and Xorg, then [`guest/run-tests.sh`](guest/run-tests.sh) runs `glxinfo -B`,
   `eglinfo -B`, `vulkaninfo --summary`, ~20 s of glmark2 and ~20 s of vkmark on the GPU, and then
   `glxinfo`, `vulkaninfo`, glmark2 and vkmark again with `LIBGL_ALWAYS_SOFTWARE=1` and only
   lavapipe, prints it all on the serial console and powers off;
4. prints one summary block to paste back: host, guest, renderers, scores with the GPU and in
   software, and what went wrong.

Every process it starts runs in its own session and is stopped when it exits, Ctrl-C included,
and its work directory (`~/.cache/agentbox-chv-gpu/run.*`) is removed unless `--keep`. Downloads
stay cached in `~/.cache/agentbox-chv-gpu`; delete it to free 1.5 GB. AgentBox's own VM, its
files, sockets and processes aren't touched, and it can run at the same time.

## Tests

```bash
scripts/chv-gpu/test/parse_test.sh        # the parsing and the summary, against fixtures/
scripts/chv-gpu/test/chv_args_test.sh     # the tarball's binaries on try.sh's and AgentBox's command lines
scripts/chv-gpu/test/seed_test.sh         # the cloud-init seed, with each tool installed
scripts/chv-gpu/test/guest-in-qemu.sh     # the guest half under QEMU, no GPU or KVM needed
```

`chv_args_test.sh` proves the tarball's Cloud Hypervisor parses and validates the command lines
try.sh (`chv_command`) and AgentBox's VM (`chArgs`, with the GPU and without, written by the Go
test `TestWriteCHArgs`) give it, with no KVM, and that upstream's v53.0 says exactly the same of
AgentBox's line without the GPU. Cloud Hypervisor opens `/dev/kvm` and checks its API version
before it reads its options, so the test runs it in a user and mount namespace where `/dev/kvm` is
an empty file, under [`fake-kvm`](test/fake-kvm.c). That ptrace supervisor answers
`KVM_GET_API_VERSION` and lets every other KVM ioctl fail. The first one after parsing, as the VM
is created, ends the run and proves the options got through. The test also checks that the harness
catches an unknown option and vhost-user without shared memory, and that crosvm takes try.sh's
and AgentBox's `--params`. It needs `gcc`, `go` and unprivileged user namespaces.

`guest-in-qemu.sh` boots the same image, seed and guest script under QEMU with its 2D virtio GPU:
cloud-init, the packages, Xorg, the framing and the summary are checked; the GPU runs fall back to
llvmpipe or fail, as they should with no 3D.

## Known not to work, or not tried

- **NVIDIA's proprietary driver and Venus**: Venus needs the host's Vulkan driver to export and
  import dma-bufs (`VK_EXT_external_memory_dma_buf`, `VK_EXT_image_drm_format_modifier`), which
  NVIDIA's driver doesn't support, so Vulkan in the guest fails. virgl (OpenGL) goes through
  EGL/GBM, which NVIDIA supports from driver 495; it's untested. Nouveau/NVK is untested too.
- **Blobs must be fds**: Spectrum's patchset handles only `SHMEM_MAP` from crosvm (map this fd
  into the guest), not `EXTERNAL_MAP` (a pointer into crosvm's memory) or `GPU_MAP` (Vulkan
  memory by device UUID). So try.sh turns on crosvm's `external-blob`, and virglrenderer is built
  with `minigbm_allocation`: GL buffers the guest maps are GBM buffers exported as dma-bufs (the
  host's GL needs `GL_EXT_memory_object_fd`), and Venus's are dma-bufs when the host's Vulkan
  driver exports them (RADV and ANV do). A blob that can't be exported fails to map in the guest
  and the summary counts it; without `external-blob`, the first such blob (resource 23 on an RX
  6750 XT) made Cloud Hypervisor drop the device and crosvm panic.
- **Which GPU**: `--render-node` (default `renderD128`; `--check` lists them) picks the host GPU,
  and AgentBox picks a discrete GPU before one on the CPU (`pickRenderNode`;
  `AGENTBOX_VM_RENDER_NODE=renderD129` in the environment `agentbox vm start` runs in picks another).
  - **GL:** our crosvm patch's `render-node` passes the node to rutabaga as a GPU path, and
    rutabaga (also patched: 0.1.75 rejected every render node, because `Path::starts_with` compares
    whole components) hands virglrenderer its fd. With `surfaceless` off, EGL comes from the GBM
    device on that node. crosvm.log says `virglrenderer: using GPU path "/dev/dri/renderD…"`, and
    the summary repeats it.
  - **Vulkan:** our virglrenderer patch holds Venus to the GPU on `VKR_RENDER_NODE`, which try.sh
    and AgentBox's supervisor set to the same node in crosvm's environment, and the render server
    inherits: the instance lists only the physical devices on that node (`VK_EXT_physical_device_drm`)
    and the device groups made of them. Unpatched, Venus listed every host GPU, an integrated one
    too. The summary's `Venus GPUs:` counts them. The guest still puts the chosen GPU first, before
    llvmpipe (Mesa's device-select layer, in the guest; AgentBox's agents get `MESA_VK_DEVICE_SELECT`
    in their profile from what the supervisor tells the VM).
  - `--isolate-gpu` (try.sh only) also runs crosvm where `/dev/dri` holds only that node. It's an
    experiment: on an RX 6750 XT, vrend's winsys failed to initialise there and GL and Venus both
    fell back to software.
  - **Not** Mesa's device-select layer on the host: in the render server it breaks Venus (vkr
    fails `vkEnumeratePhysicalDeviceGroups` with `ERROR_INITIALIZATION_FAILED`). Nor `DRI_PRIME`:
    virglrenderer's node choice ignores it, and that same layer reads it. The guest still puts the
    chosen GPU first with the layer, in the guest, where it's harmless.
  - **The summary** says where each ran: GL from the render node crosvm had open (by device number), Vulkan from the
    vendor:device vkmark used. It flags either one not on the chosen node.
- **Fences after a GL query**: virglrenderer, as rutabaga sets it up (a sync thread, async fence
  callbacks), retires a fence while a query is pending only once the device has called
  `virgl_renderer_poll()`, which it asks for on an eventfd. crosvm's in-process GPU polls that fd;
  its vhost-user backend, the one Cloud Hypervisor uses, didn't, so the first fence after a GL
  query (Chromium and Xvnc's glamor make them) never signalled, nor did any after it: every draw in
  the guest hung in `dma_fence_default_wait`, and crosvm logged `timeout (5s) waiting for renderer
  poll() to finish` every 5 s. glmark2 and vkmark make no queries, so the spike never hit it. Our
  crosvm patch `0002` polls it; the guest's `query-fence-gpu` check (guest/query-fence.c) makes a
  query and then waits on a fence, and the summary's `GL query+fence:` says whether it returned.
- **No display**: crosvm runs with its stub display, so the guest has a scanout (its X server
  works) but nothing is shown on the host. AgentBox's agents draw on their own virtual displays,
  so it's what we'd want, but crosvm's Wayland/X display paths aren't exercised.
- **virgl's OpenGL** tops out at what virglrenderer translates (OpenGL 4.3 / GLES 3.2 on most
  hosts) and costs a copy per frame; Venus is near native but needs a guest kernel 5.16 or later
  with blob resources and context init (Debian 13's 6.12 has them).
- **Spectrum's patchset** was written for crosvm's cross-domain (Wayland) contexts, Spectrum's
  use; virgl and Venus over it ran on the user's RX 6750 XT with the v50 build. Snapshot, restore
  and live migration of a VM with the GPU device weren't tried, nor was `ch-remote add-gpu`
  (AgentBox gives the device only as the VM starts).
- **amd64 only**, see build.sh above.

# agentbox-hub

The AgentBox hub: puts every machine running AgentBox in one place.

```sh
npx agentbox-hub
```

With no flags it runs on SQLite in a data directory, with no config, and prints a one-time setup link and a QR code. Whoever opens the link first becomes the owner.

- `--listen 0.0.0.0:8080` to reach it from other machines.
- `--url https://hub.example.com` for the address it puts in links.

`npx agentbox-hub --help` lists the rest.

The binary comes in a per-platform package (`@agentbox-hub/<os>-<cpu>`) installed as an optional dependency: linux, macOS and Windows on x64 and arm64. Don't install with `--omit=optional`. Set `AGENTBOX_HUB_BINARY` to run a binary of your own.

# Patches

Applied by the Dockerfile in name order, each directory to its project. Every Linux VM runs the
Cloud Hypervisor they make, with "GPU for agents" on or off.

## vhost/: rust-vmm's vhost crates at vhost-user-backend-v0.22.0 (vhost 0.16.0), as Cloud Hypervisor v53.0 uses them

Spectrum OS's `vhost.patch` (50.0-spectrum0), rebased from vhost-user-backend-v0.20.0:

- `0001-vhost_user-add-get_size-to-MsgHeader.patch`: applied as is.
- `0002-vhost-fix-receiving-reply-payloads.patch`: applied as is.
- `0003-vhost_user-add-shared-memory-region-support.patch`: crosvm's non-standard shared-memory
  messages: `GET_SHARED_MEMORY_REGIONS` (front end, 1004), `SHMEM_MAP` and `SHMEM_UNMAP` (back
  end, 1000 and 1001). v0.22 has since standardised its own `SHMEM_MAP`/`SHMEM_UNMAP` (9 and 10,
  with a different body, `VhostUserMMap`) and `GET_SHMEM_CONFIG` (44), which crosvm 18bc84d0
  doesn't speak. Those are left as they are; crosvm's are added beside them, renamed
  `CROSVM_SHMEM_MAP`/`CROSVM_SHMEM_UNMAP` and handled by new `crosvm_shmem_map`/`crosvm_shmem_unmap`
  methods. Only crosvm's always get a reply, as the patch had it.
- `0004-vhost_user-add-protocol-flag-for-shmem.patch`: the protocol bit (`0x8000_0000`) after
  v0.22's new ones.

Nothing in Cloud Hypervisor sends or accepts any of these but the GPU device, which only exists
with `--gpu`.

## cloud-hypervisor/: Cloud Hypervisor v53.0

Spectrum OS's `cloud-hypervisor.patch` (50.0-spectrum0), rebased from v50.0:

- `0001-build-use-local-vhost.patch`: points the workspace at the patched vhost crates;
  `default-features = false` kept, as v53 has it.
- `0002-virtio-devices-add-a-GPU-device.patch`: `--gpu socket=…`, `ch-remote add-gpu`,
  `/vm.add-gpu`, and the vhost-user GPU device with its 8 GiB shared-memory BAR. Rebased onto
  v53's APIs: `GpuConfig` takes the flattened `PciDeviceCommonConfig` (`id`, `pci_segment`,
  `pci_device_id`) and Landlock rules as v53's `FsConfig` does; the device follows v53's
  `VirtioDevice` (`ActivationContext`, `VhostUserCommon` holding `VirtioCommon`, `spawn_worker`,
  `reset`); it is added beside v53's new generic vhost-user device wherever both register; and
  `ActivateError::VhostUserGpuSetup` gets its own message, which had taken `CreateSeccompFilter`'s.
  Beyond the GPU, it changes `VirtioSharedMemoryList::region_list` from a `Vec` to a `BTreeMap`
  keyed by shmid, read only by the PCI transport and set only by the GPU device (virtio-fs's cache
  is always `None` in v53).

Spectrum's backport of upstream 57e766bd (no double activation with 2+ vCPUs, issue #7766) isn't
needed: it is in v52.0 and so in v53.0.

The binary is built as upstream's `cloud-hypervisor-static` is (`--all --release --features
mshv`, musl), with `CH_EXTRA_VERSION=agentbox-<hash of the build's inputs>`: it says `v53.0.0-agentbox-<hash>`.
`test/chv_args_test.sh` runs it and upstream's own v53.0 on AgentBox's VM's command line without
the GPU and checks they say the same.

## crosvm/: crosvm 18bc84d0, the commit Spectrum tested the patchset with

- `0001-gpu-render-node-parameter.patch`: ours, not upstream (crosvm's main has no equivalent). A
  `render-node` key in `device gpu --params`, added as a GPU path for rutabaga, which hands its fd
  to virglrenderer (`get_drm_fd`). Without it virglrenderer renders GL on the first
  `/dev/dri/renderD*` that `readdir` returns: on a machine with an integrated and a discrete GPU,
  the integrated one. crosvm runs with `"surfaceless": false` too, since a surfaceless EGL
  display is Mesa's default device whatever the fd.

- `0002-vhost-user-gpu-poll-the-renderer.patch`: ours, not upstream (crosvm's main doesn't have it
  either). The vhost-user GPU backend never polled virglrenderer's poll descriptor, which the
  in-process device does (`WorkerToken::VirtioGpuPoll`). With async fence callbacks, a fence while
  a GL query is pending waits for that poll, so the first fence after a query never signalled, and
  no fence after it did either. The patch adds a platform worker that calls `event_poll` whenever the
  descriptor is readable, on the backend's executor thread as the control queue's worker runs.

## virglrenderer/: virglrenderer 1.2.0

- `0001-venus-render-node.patch`: ours. `VKR_RENDER_NODE` in the render server's environment (it
  inherits crosvm's) holds Venus to that render node's GPU: the instance lists only the physical
  devices whose `VK_EXT_physical_device_drm` render node it is, and `vkEnumeratePhysicalDeviceGroups`
  only the groups made wholly of those, since a group with another device in it fails vkr's lookup of
  its handles. When no device matches (a driver without the extension), the filter is off and the
  render server logs it. Mesa's device-select layer can't do this in the render server: there it
  makes `vkEnumeratePhysicalDeviceGroups` fail.

## rutabaga_gfx/: the crates.io crate rutabaga_gfx 0.1.75, which crosvm renders with

Fetched at the version and checksum crosvm's Cargo.lock pins, then used from a path, with cargo
offline from there.

- `0001-accept-render-node-gpu-paths.patch`: ours. `is_valid_gpu_path` checked
  `Path::starts_with("/dev/dri/renderD")`, which compares whole components, so no render node was
  ever accepted and `get_drm_fd` always fell back to virglrenderer's own pick. The patch compares
  the path as a string (with a unit test the build runs, `test/render-node-path.sh`), and logs the
  path it takes (`virglrenderer: using GPU path …`), or that there was none. Confirmed on the
  user's RX 6750 XT: GL and Venus both on it.

## Moving to a newer Cloud Hypervisor

1. Clone it and rust-vmm/vhost at the tags it uses (its `Cargo.toml`), apply these series with
   `git am -3`, and fix what conflicts: in v50 → v53, 55 conflict hunks in the GPU commit, nearly all
   of them a new upstream device (the generic vhost-user one) registered where the GPU one is, plus
   the `VirtioDevice` API change, which meant porting `gpu.rs` after `vhost_user/fs.rs`.
2. `cargo clippy`, and `cargo test -p vmm -p virtio-devices -p cloud-hypervisor` (the tests that
   need `/dev/kvm` fail without it, as upstream's do).
3. `git format-patch` into these directories, bump `CHV_VERSION` in `versions.env`, run `build.sh`
   and `test/chv_args_test.sh` here, and `try.sh` on a machine with KVM and a GPU. Merged, the
   Cloud Hypervisor workflow publishes the build and opens the pull request that pins it.
4. Watch upstream for the GPU: if crosvm moves to the standard vhost-user shared-memory messages,
   or Cloud Hypervisor grows them, `vhost/0003` and most of `0002` can go.

# Contributing to AgentBox

## Read this first

AgentBox is young, and where it goes is still being decided. Contributions are welcome, but the ones
most likely to land are small and focused:

- a bug fix, with a test that fails without it;
- a reliability or performance fix you can show the before and after of;
- a correction to the docs, where they say something the code doesn't do.

Less likely to land: large pull requests, new features nobody asked for, rewrites, and anything that
widens what AgentBox is for. **If you want to build something bigger, open an issue first** and say
what you have in mind. It saves you writing something that won't be merged.

Opening a pull request doesn't oblige anyone to merge it. It may be closed, asked to shrink, or
reimplemented differently later.

## What you need

- **Linux on x86_64.** AgentBox runs its agents in [Incus](https://linuxcontainers.org/incus/)
  containers, and Incus is Linux-only. Arch, Debian 12 or 13, Ubuntu 22.04 or newer, and Fedora are
  known to work. macOS and Windows aren't supported.
- **[mise](https://mise.jdx.dev/)**, for Go and Node. [`mise.toml`](mise.toml) pins them: `mise install`
  in the checkout installs Go 1.27, Node LTS and the rest.
- **`/dev/kvm`**, to run agents at all: on Linux, AgentBox runs in a Cloud Hypervisor VM of its own,
  which `bin/agentbox vm init` makes, with no password. Unit tests and the desktop build don't need
  it.
- A **Claude Code, Codex or OpenCode** login, if you want an agent to do real work.

## Build and run it

```bash
git clone https://github.com/leciric/agentbox.git
cd agentbox
mise install

go build -o bin/agentbox ./cmd/agentbox      # the CLI and the daemon, one binary; reports "agentbox version dev"
bin/agentbox vm init                         # AgentBox's VM, once per machine; it runs this same binary
bin/agentbox image build                     # the agents' base image, built in the VM in a few minutes
bin/agentbox auth claude                     # runs `claude setup-token`
```

**The daemon** is the same binary, in the VM. Any command starts it on demand, in the background, and
every command but `agentbox vm …` runs in the VM, which gets the binary that ran it; to watch the
daemon's log, run it in the foreground instead:

```bash
bin/agentbox daemon stop      # if a command already started one
bin/agentbox daemon           # serves ~/.local/share/agentbox/run/agentbox.sock, forwarded from the VM
```

To run AgentBox on the machine itself instead, the way the VM does inside, set
`AGENTBOX_FRONT_END=host` and set the machine up once with `sudo bash scripts/host-setup.sh` (Incus,
the firewall rules and the UID mapping). That is what CI's base image workflow does; it isn't offered
to users.

**The CLI** talks to that socket:

```bash
bin/agentbox add ~/src/my-project
bin/agentbox create my-project
bin/agentbox chat my-project/agent-01 "Why does the login fail?"
bin/agentbox list
```

**The desktop app** is an Electron client of the same socket. Point it at the binary you built:

```bash
npm --prefix desktop install
cd desktop && AGENTBOX_BIN=$PWD/../bin/agentbox npm start
```

`npm --prefix desktop run dist` builds `bin/agentbox` with the version in `desktop/package.json`, and
the AppImage, `.deb` and `.pacman` in `desktop/dist/`. `bin/` is gitignored: rebuild after pulling.

Before you change anything, read [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md): the short tour of the codebase that
AgentBox's own agents are given, and a good one for people too.

## Tests

```bash
go vet ./...
go test ./...                               # everything that runs without Incus
npm --prefix desktop run typecheck
npm --prefix desktop run build
```

- **Integration tests** are behind the `integration` build tag. They create real Incus containers, so
  they need a host set up with `scripts/host-setup.sh` and the base image built with
  `bin/agentbox image build`. They skip what they can't reach (a base image that isn't built, a
  display for the browser tests, `opencode` if it isn't installed). They can't run inside an AgentBox
  agent, which has no Incus.

  ```bash
  go test -tags integration ./internal/agent
  go test -tags integration -p 1 ./internal/daemon ./internal/agent
  ```

- **The API types are generated.** The renderer's types in
  [`desktop/src/shared/api.ts`](desktop/src/shared/api.ts) come from `internal/api`. Change
  `internal/api` and `TestTypeScriptTypesAreUpToDate` fails until you regenerate them:

  ```bash
  UPDATE_TS=1 go test ./internal/api
  ```

- **The agent's brief has golden files.** Change
  [`internal/brief/brief.md.tmpl`](internal/brief/brief.md.tmpl) and update them:

  ```bash
  go test ./internal/brief -update
  ```

- **Demo scripts** in [`scripts/demo/`](scripts/demo/) check features end to end. Many need no
  Incus and no login: they stand up a throwaway daemon with a stub `incus` and drive the real app.
  The comment at the top of each script says what it needs and how to run it.

## The rail and the sidebar

Both are narrow, fixed-width columns filled with whatever agents write, so a long path, an unbroken
URL or a `<pre>` without `min-w-0` drags them wider than they're allowed to be. A preview harness
stands both up against fixtures made to trigger exactly that:

```bash
npm --prefix desktop run preview                                    # serve it, print the URL
npm --prefix desktop run preview -- --shots out                     # screenshot every scenario into out/
npm --prefix desktop run preview -- --shots out --against HEAD~1    # and diff against another commit
```

The scenarios are in `desktop/src/renderer/dev/scenarios.json`. If Playwright can't launch its
browser, run `npx playwright install chromium` once. If your change touches either column, put the
before and after in your pull request.

## Conventions

- **Conventional commits:** `feat: ...`, `fix: ...`, `refactor: ...`, `docs: ...`, `test: ...`,
  `chore: ...`.
- **Migrations are appended, never edited.** `migrations` in
  [`internal/state/state.go`](internal/state/state.go) is one ordered list, tracked with
  `PRAGMA user_version`. Editing a past entry leaves already-migrated databases behind.
- **Record a decision** in your pull request when the shape of something is worth recording: the
  context, what was decided, what was rejected, and what proves it. Code comments cite earlier
  decisions by number (D1–D90); their records aren't in this repository.
- **Explain a feature worth explaining** in its pull request: what it does, what was checked, where
  the code is, and what it still can't do.
- **The desktop app stays a thin client.** Its main process relays the daemon's socket to the
  renderer and nothing else: AgentBox logic, Incus and git belong in the daemon.
- **Changing [`internal/image/provision.sh`](internal/image/provision.sh) means bumping
  `image.Version`** in [`internal/image/image.go`](internal/image/image.go). That is what tells Setup
  the installed image is outdated. The [Base image](.github/workflows/base-image.yml) workflow
  builds it on every change to `internal/image/`, and publishes nothing: every machine builds its
  own image, because it holds software we may not redistribute. `sudo scripts/check-personalise.sh` checks `personalise.sh`
  without Incus.

## The hub

The hub, the server half behind remote environments, is a separate program in [`hub/`](hub/)
(`npx agentbox-hub`), built and tested with the rest. The protocol between the two halves is
[`hubapi/`](hubapi/): the hub imports it and nothing else of AgentBox, and `internal/` never
imports anything from the hub. A change to `hubapi/` is checked against both sides by the same
`go test`.

## Pull requests

1. Branch from `main` and keep the change to one thing. Don't mix unrelated fixes.
2. Run `go vet ./...`, `go test ./...` and the desktop `typecheck` and `build` before you push.
3. Say what changed and why, and how you checked it. If you can't say how you checked it, it isn't
   ready.
4. For anything visible in the app, include before-and-after screenshots; for something that moves
   or is a flow, a short recording.
5. If the change alters how something works, say so, and record the decision if the shape of it
   changed.

[CI](.github/workflows/ci.yml) runs on every pull request: `go vet ./...`,
`go vet -tags integration ./...` and `go test ./...` in one job, and `npm ci`, `typecheck` and `build`
for the desktop app in another. It doesn't run the integration tests (GitHub's runners have no
Incus) or package the AppImage; both are yours to check when your change touches them.

Releases are made by the maintainer from `main`, as described in [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md#releasing).

## Reporting bugs

[Open an issue](https://github.com/leciric/agentbox/issues/new/choose) with the version (`agentbox
--version`, or the AppImage's name), your distribution, what you did, and what happened. The
daemon's log is `~/.local/share/agentbox/daemon.log`. **Redact tokens, API keys and private paths**
before you paste it.

A security problem doesn't belong in a public issue: contact the maintainer privately first.

# Security

## Reporting a vulnerability

Please report vulnerabilities privately, not in a public issue: open the repository's
[Security tab](https://github.com/leciric/agentbox/security) and choose **Report a vulnerability**
(GitHub's private vulnerability reporting). Say what you found, how to reproduce it, and what it
lets someone do. You'll get an answer there, and the fix and its advisory are published once a
release carries it.

## What's in scope

- **The daemon**: `agentbox` and its HTTP API on the unix socket, the state it keeps, and anything
  that lets another local user or process drive it.
- **The agents' machines and their sandboxing**: an agent reaching the host, another agent's
  machine, worktree or network, or anything outside what it was given.
- **Tokens and credentials**: GitHub tokens, AI tools' logins and API keys, and anything else
  AgentBox stores, passes to agents or could leak through logs, media or the app.

Bugs in the AI tools themselves (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode) belong to their own projects.

## Supported versions

Only the [latest release](https://downloads.agentbox.linting.dev/index.html) gets security fixes.
