# An agent's lifecycle

[← back to the index](README.md)

An agent is a git worktree, a branch, an Incus container and a tmux session with an AI tool
running in it, all created together by `agentbox create` and torn down together by
`agentbox destroy`.

## What an agent is

The `Agent` row (`internal/state/state.go`) has, among others:

- `Project`, `Name` — identity.
- `Instance` — the Incus container name, `"ab-<project>-<agent>"` (`internal/agent/agent.go`).
- `Branch` — the git branch: the project's branch prefix (`agentbox/` unless it was changed) and the agent's name.
- `Worktree` — the host path, `~/.local/share/agentbox/worktrees/<project>/<agent>`
  (`internal/paths`).
- `Status` — `AgentCreating` or `AgentReady` (`state.go`). This is not the container's power
  state: `agentbox stop`/`pause`/`resume` (`internal/agent/agent.go`, `Manager.Stop`/`Pause`/
  `Resume`) act on the Incus instance directly (`incus stop`/`pause`/`resume`) and don't change
  this column.
- `AI` — which tool it runs: `"claude"`, `"codex"`, `"opencode"`, or `"none"`.
- `Autonomous` — whether its AI tool starts unattended.
- `Role` — `RoleWorker` for a normal agent, or `RoleLead` for the project's chat, which has no
  Incus instance at all (see [The lead and its MCP tools](lead.md)).
- `ClaudeAccount`, `GitHubAccount`, `Interface`, `FinishNotice` — configuration.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> creating: agentbox create
    creating --> ready: build() succeeds
    creating --> [*]: build() fails, undo functions unwind
    ready --> running: incus start (default after create)
    running --> stopped: agentbox stop
    running --> paused: agentbox pause
    paused --> running: agentbox resume
    stopped --> running: agentbox start
    ready --> destroyed: agentbox destroy
    running --> destroyed: agentbox destroy
    stopped --> destroyed: agentbox destroy
```

`Status` only ever holds the top row of the diagram (`creating`/`ready`); the container states
below it (`running`/`stopped`/`paused`) are read from Incus, not from `state.db`.

## `create_agent`, end to end

Creating an agent is triggered from the lead over its `create_agent` MCP tool (see
[The lead and its MCP tools](lead.md)), or from the CLI/app calling the same daemon endpoint
directly.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Lead as Lead (MCP create_agent)
    participant API as Daemon HTTP API
    participant Mgr as agent.Manager (internal/agent)
    participant Git as internal/gitrepo
    participant Incus as internal/incus
    participant Container as Agent's container

    Lead->>API: create_agent(name?, ai, ...)
    API->>Mgr: createAgentFrom() -> Create() -> build()
    Mgr->>Mgr: pick agent name, build Instance/Branch/Worktree names
    Mgr->>Mgr: store agent row, status = creating
    Mgr->>Git: AddWorktree(path, branch, commit)
    Git-->>Mgr: git worktree add -b <branch> <path> <commit>
    Mgr->>Incus: copy agentbox-base/ready (or project's own base) -> instance
    Incus->>Container: incus copy, mount worktree + .git as disk devices
    Mgr->>Incus: start instance
    Incus->>Container: incus start
    Mgr->>Container: wait for boot + IPv4 (WaitReady, 2 minute timeout)
    Mgr->>Container: verify git mount (git rev-parse --git-dir), fix ownership
    Mgr->>Container: push in-agent API binary, configure git/logins/brief
    Mgr->>Container: start tmux session "main", launch AI tool in window 1
    Mgr->>Incus: snapshot "initial"
    Mgr->>Mgr: status = ready
    Mgr-->>API: Agent
    API-->>Lead: Agent
```

Steps, from `build()` in `internal/agent/agent.go`:

1. Pick an agent name if none was given (next free `agent-NN`), and derive `Instance`, `Branch`
   and `Worktree`.
2. Validate the name and check the branch and worktree don't already exist.
3. Store the agent row with `Status = AgentCreating`, registering an undo function.
4. For a Claude Code agent, save its chat defaults.
5. Create the git worktree and branch: `internal/gitrepo`'s `AddWorktree(path, branch, commit)`
   runs `git worktree add --quiet -b <branch> <path> <commit>`; its undo removes the worktree and
   deletes the branch.
6. Optionally copy env files into the worktree.
7. Create the Incus container: copy from a snapshot (the project's own saved base, or
   `agentbox-base/ready` — see [The base image](base-image.md)), strip devices carried over from
   the clone, mount the worktree and its `.git` as disk devices so git crosses the container
   boundary, and start it. `WaitReady()` (`internal/incus`) waits up to
   two minutes for systemd and an IPv4 address.
8. Verify the git mount works (`git rev-parse --git-dir` as the agent user) and fix `.git`
   ownership for tools that write next to it.
9. Push the in-agent API binary and set up its proxy device (`internal/agent/agentapi.go`).
10. Configure git, logins and render the brief into the container (`configure()`; see
    [Project notes and the brief](notes-and-brief.md)).
11. Start the tmux session: `ensureSession()` creates a session named `"main"` with a shell
    window, and — for a CLI-interfaced agent — a second window running the AI tool
    (`toolWindowScript()` in `internal/agent/chat.go`), with an `--autonomous` variant when
    `Autonomous` is set.
12. Take an Incus snapshot named `"initial"`.
13. Set `Status = AgentReady` and return the agent.

Any failure before the last step unwinds through the undo functions registered along the way
(dropping the worktree/branch, the database row, and so on), so a failed create doesn't leave a
half-built agent behind.

## Goals

An agent can have a goal: what done looks like, with checks AgentBox runs itself each time the
agent ends a turn — an open pull request (`pr_open`), green CI on it (`ci_green`), or a shell
command that must exit 0 in its worktree. While a check fails, the agent is sent back with what
is missing, up to its budget (10 times by default, at most 50). When every check passes the goal
is met and the agent finishes as usual; when the budget runs out, or the agent ends a message
with `GOAL BLOCKED: <what it needs>`, the goal is blocked and the agent waits for you.

- **When creating a task**: the New task form's Goal, `agentbox create --goal "…" --goal-check …`,
  or `create_agent`'s `goal` from the project's chat or the Home chat.
- **On an agent that exists**: its page's Goal card (set, edit, clear),
  `agentbox goal <project/agent> "…" --check ci_green`, the project chat's `tell_agent` with a
  `goal`, or the Home chat's `set_goal`. An idle or finished agent goes back to work on it; a
  working one reads it mid-turn. A new goal replaces the old one with its whole budget, and
  `agentbox goal <project/agent> --clear` stops the checks.
- **The AI tool's own `/goal`** (Claude Code, Codex), typed in an agent's chat, shows as its goal
  too; the tool checks it itself, and it is cleared with `/goal clear` in the chat.

`agentbox list` shows each agent's goal state, and `agentbox goal <project/agent>` its checks and
budget left.

## Jobs

Anything this slow runs as a job (`internal/daemon/jobs.go`), so the caller isn't blocked and can
follow progress over the event stream or `GET /v1/jobs`:

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> running: jobs.start()
    running --> succeeded: handler returns nil
    running --> failed: handler returns an error
    running --> cancelled: caller cancels
    succeeded --> [*]
    failed --> [*]
    cancelled --> [*]
```

`create_agent`, `agentbox image build`, and taking or restoring a snapshot are all jobs; their
result is persisted to the `jobs` table (`internal/state`) once they finish, and the job status
matches `internal/api/types.go`'s `JobRunning`/`JobSucceeded`/`JobFailed`/`JobCancelled`.

AgentBox is a Go daemon and CLI (`cmd/agentbox`, `internal/`) plus an Electron desktop app
(`desktop/`). The daemon is the only thing that touches Incus, git or the database; the CLI and
the desktop app are both clients of its HTTP API over a unix socket.

## The daemon

[`internal/daemon`](../internal/daemon) is the control plane. `daemon.New(daemon.Config{...})`
builds a `Server` (`server.go`) holding the SQLite store, an event broker, a jobs manager, chat
sessions and the HTTP servers; `srv.Run(ctx)` starts it. It's launched by `internal/cli/daemon.go`,
directly or auto-started by any CLI command that needs it.

The daemon claims a unix socket at `~/.local/share/agentbox/run/agentbox.sock` (checked and
locked in `server.go` so two daemons can't run at once), and serves over 50 routes under `/v1/`
through a plain `http.ServeMux` (`server.routes()`), each handler wrapped to turn a returned error
into a JSON error response.

**Jobs** are how the daemon runs anything slow — creating an agent, building the base image,
running a snapshot — without blocking a request. Defined in
[`internal/daemon/jobs.go`](../internal/daemon/jobs.go): starting a job runs it in a goroutine,
publishes events as it progresses, and persists the result to the `jobs` table. A client polls
`GET /v1/jobs` or follows the event stream. See [An agent's lifecycle](agent-lifecycle.md) for the
job state diagram.

## The API

[`internal/api`](../internal/api) defines the wire types (`types.go`: `Project`, `Agent`, `Job`,
`ChatEvent`, memory types, and more) and a client (`client.go`) that dials the unix socket — or,
for a hub-connected project, an HTTPS base URL with a bearer token (`NewRemoteClient`). Handlers
in the daemon and the client both share these types, so there's one definition of the wire format.

The desktop app's TypeScript types are generated from these Go types, not hand-maintained.
`TestTypeScriptTypesAreUpToDate` in [`internal/api/typescript_test.go`](../internal/api/typescript_test.go)
reflects over the structs and constants listed there and writes
[`desktop/src/shared/api.ts`](../desktop/src/shared/api.ts); the test fails if the checked-in file
is stale, and `UPDATE_TS=1 go test ./internal/api` regenerates it after you change
`internal/api/types.go`.

## The CLI

[`internal/cli`](../internal/cli), entered from `cmd/agentbox/main.go` via `NewRootCmd()`
(`root.go`), is a client of the daemon's socket: `app.client()` builds an `api.Client` against it,
auto-starting the daemon (`a.startDaemon()`) if nothing answers, and restarting a stale one
(wrong version, or missing the `incus-admin`/`kvm` group) when no job is running.

Command groups include: project management (`add`, `projects`, `project`, `remove`, `notes`,
`brief`), agents (`create`, `list`, `retire`, `destroy`, `start`, `stop`, `pause`, `resume`),
communication (`shell`, `exec`, `chat`, `ask`, `questions`), auth (`auth`, `claude`, `github`),
utilities (`daemon`, `jobs`, `events`, `media`, `tokens`, `limits`), desktop-related
(`desktop`, `browser`, `android`, `ios`), the base image (`image`), and hub/remote (`env`, `login`,
`logout`).

## The desktop app is a thin client

- `desktop/src/main` is the Electron main process. It only relays the socket to the renderer —
  it holds no AgentBox logic, doesn't shell out to Incus or git, and doesn't touch the database.
  `connection.ts` builds the request options (socket path, or an HTTPS hub URL with a stored
  token) and manages hub credentials via the OS keyring.
- `desktop/src/preload` is the bridge exposed to the renderer through `contextBridge`:
  `agentbox.request()` for API calls, `agentbox.stream.*` for the WebSocket terminal/log streams,
  plus narrow helpers for the CLI, host setup, hubs and media (`agentbox-media://`).
- `desktop/src/renderer` is the React UI (Tailwind, Radix, xterm.js, noVNC). It never talks to the
  daemon directly — only through `window.agentbox.*` from the preload bridge — and imports its
  API types from the generated `desktop/src/shared/api.ts`.

A hub is the optional server half of AgentBox, a separate program in [`hub/`](../hub)

  `abx_p_` for a pairing's secret, `abx_l_` for a setup link's), the session cookie name, the hub's
  own endpoints (`/v1/hub`, `/v1/setup`, `/v1/pair`, `/v1/pairings`, `/v1/devices`,

  `EnvironmentAPI(id)` — the prefix under which a hub passes a
  request through to that environment's daemon, exactly as it would arrive over the daemon's own
  socket.
- `tunnel.go` frames the WebSocket tunnel an environment dials to a hub.
- `types.go` is the shared request/response shapes.

Nothing in `internal/` imports anything from the hub itself — only from `hubapi/`. How to run one
and connect to it: [A hub](hub.md).

# The base image

[← back to the index](README.md)

Every agent's container starts life as a clone of a shared Incus snapshot, `agentbox-base/ready`
(or a project's own saved base), rather than being provisioned from scratch each time — see
[An agent's lifecycle](agent-lifecycle.md).

## Building it

[`internal/image`](../internal/image) tracks the image with a version string, `image.Version`
(`image.go`). `agentbox image build`, or Setup's **Build base image**, makes it and snapshots it as
`agentbox-base/ready`:

- **With no optional component**, it downloads the image AgentBox publishes for that version from
  `https://downloads.agentbox.linting.dev/images/`, or from the `image-<version>` release at
  `https://github.com/leciric/agentbox/releases` when that fails, a few parts at a time, checks them
  against the release's `SHA256SUMS`, joins them and imports the image into Incus. It is compressed
  with zstd, which Incus unpacks several times faster than gzip. A download that is interrupted
  (the connection drops, AgentBox restarts or the build is cancelled) carries on from where it got to
  the next time. `AGENTBOX_IMAGES_URL` in the daemon's environment points it somewhere else (several
  URLs, separated by spaces, are tried in order). That image is Debian 13 with
  [`provision.sh`](../internal/image/provision.sh) applied and every tool in `tools.txt` except
  Claude Code, its ACP adapter and Cursor's SDK, which AgentBox may not redistribute: the machine
  installs those itself, at their `tools.txt` versions, before making the image its own.
- **With a component** (Codex, OpenCode, the Android tools, the development caches, Incus), with
  `agentbox image build --local`, with `AGENTBOX_IMAGES_URL=off` in the daemon's environment, or
  when the download or its checksum fails, it builds the image here instead, from
  `images:debian/13`, by running `provision.sh` against a fresh container, which takes a few
  minutes longer. The build log says which it did and why.

Only the newest image version is published, so an AgentBox older than the latest image builds its
own. The image release is a prerelease, never marked latest, so it doesn't show up as an AgentBox
update. Next to each image are `packages-<arch>.txt`, its Debian packages with their exact versions, and
`SOURCES-<arch>.md`, where the source of each is on snapshot.debian.org and the licenses of the agent tools
in it.

**Changing `provision.sh` means bumping `image.Version`**: that's what tells an existing
machine's Setup page the installed image is outdated, and asks for a rebuild.

A new AgentBox that only moves the agent tools on (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, the GitHub CLI
and the like) doesn't ask for a rebuild: on start, the daemon updates them in the base image in
place, in the background, installing only the tools that changed and checking every one. Setup
says "Updating agent tools…" while it runs, and new agents are made from the current image until
the updated one is in place. If the update fails, the image stays as it was and keeps working, and
Setup says why and offers **Rebuild base image**.

To get new Claude Code releases without waiting for an AgentBox release, turn on **Keep Claude Code
up to date** in Settings → Models. Once a day, and when AgentBox starts, the daemon asks npm for the
newest Claude Code and its chat adapter and updates them in the base image the same way, checking
every tool before the new image is used. Agents created after that start on the new versions;
existing agents move to them when their chat next starts, or before the next turn of a chat that
is running, never in the middle of one. If an update fails, agents keep the versions they have and
Settings says why. The version an AgentBox release ships with is the oldest it ever uses, and
turning the setting off goes back to it. **Check now** checks at once.

## What `provision.sh` sets up

Run inside the container before it's snapshotted:

- base packages — `curl`, `git`, `tmux`, `build-essential`, Docker, Python, and the rest an agent
  needs to work;
- a display stack for the desktop tools: a VNC server, Chromium, an Openbox desktop, a terminal,
  `ffmpeg` for recordings, and (opt-in, `AGENTBOX_WITH_ANDROID`) `scrcpy` for the Android emulator
  screen;
- [mise](https://mise.jdx.dev), and through it the tools pinned in `tools.txt` that every agent
  gets: Go, Node, Claude Code, the GitHub CLI, the Playwright MCP server, and Codex/OpenCode where
  requested. OpenCode 2 is not in `tools.txt` or the image: each agent installs its npm
  platform package at its first OpenCode 2 start (needs the network then) and links it as `opencode2`
  in the user's `~/.local/bin`, the host's lead does the same the first time it needs it, and the
  installation setting `opencode_version` chooses which one agents and the project chat run;
- a placeholder user, `agent` (UID/GID 1000), in the `sudo` and `docker` groups;
- a check at the end that every pinned tool actually reports the version it was asked to install.

## Docker images agents share

Agents that run Docker pull Docker Hub's images through one cache that AgentBox's daemon keeps in
its VM, on the agents' disk, so an image several agents use is downloaded and stored once. It's on
by default, holds at most 20 GiB or an eighth of its disk, whichever is less (the least recently used
images go first), and never fills the disk past its floor. A `--max` bigger than the disk can hold is
capped, with a warning.
Settings → Storage and machine → "Share Docker images between agents" turns it off, changes its size, shows
what it holds and empties it; so does `agentbox docker-cache [on|off] [--max 30GiB] [--clear]`.

- Each agent's `/etc/docker/daemon.json` lists the cache in `registry-mirrors`, at
  `http://127.0.0.1:47500` inside the agent; `docker info | grep -A2 Mirrors` shows it. Agents that
  already exist get it when they next start: no rebuild needed.
- Only Docker Hub goes through it. Images from `ghcr.io`, `quay.io` and other registries are pulled
  from them directly by every agent, because Docker's mirror setting only covers Docker Hub.
- If the cache can't answer (the daemon is restarting, or Docker Hub is unreachable from it), Docker
  pulls from Docker Hub itself, as it does whenever a mirror fails.

## Package caches agents share

Agents' package managers download into caches that AgentBox keeps in its VM and every agent shares,
so a new agent installs from what earlier ones fetched instead of downloading it all again: pnpm's
store, npm's cache and `npx`, Yarn 2+ (Berry), Go's module and build caches, pip, uv, Corepack's
package managers and Playwright's browsers. They're on the agents' disk, outlive the agents, are on
by default, hold at most 20 GiB together or an eighth of their disk, whichever is less (what was used
longest ago goes first), and never fill the disk past its floor.
Settings → Storage and machine → "Share package caches between agents" turns them off, changes their size,
shows what they hold and empties them; so does `agentbox package-cache [on|off] [--max 30GiB] [--clear]`.

- They're mounted at `/var/cache/agentbox/packages` in every agent, and the agent's environment
  points the tools there (`npm_config_cache`, `pnpm_config_store_dir`, `GOMODCACHE`, `GOCACHE`,
  `PIP_CACHE_DIR`, `UV_CACHE_DIR`, `COREPACK_HOME`, `PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH`). pnpm 10 and older
  read `~/.config/pnpm/rc`, Yarn Berry `~/.yarnrc.yml`; a value you set there yourself is kept.
  Agents that already exist get them when they next start.
- Only downloads go there. Logins, tokens, `.env` files and npm's logs stay in each agent. Every
  agent of every project reads them, though, so a private package one project installs is in the
  cache for the others too.
- Yarn 1 keeps a cache per agent, as it can't share one between agents installing at the same time.
- A project's `node_modules` is copied from pnpm's store rather than hard-linked, as the two are on
  different disks: still much faster than downloading.
- Turned off, agents go back to caches of their own when their shells next start.

## Personalising it

`agentbox-base/ready` still has the placeholder `agent` user in it when it's built.
[`personalise.sh`](../internal/image/personalise.sh) renames that user to the host's own — same
UID/GID or a new one, same group memberships and subordinate UID/GID ranges, `/etc/sudoers.d/
90-agentbox` and `/etc/subuid`/`/etc/subgid` rewritten to match — the moment before a machine
snapshots its own container as ready to clone from. It can be checked without Incus at all:
`sudo scripts/check-personalise.sh` runs it against a real Debian 13 root filesystem (pulled via
Docker) in a chroot, across cases like a plain rename, a new UID/GID, a clash with an existing
system account, and a placeholder left unchanged.

## Checking it in CI

The [Base image workflow](../.github/workflows/base-image.yml) builds the image the way a new
machine does, on pull requests that touch `internal/image/`, so a `provision.sh` change is checked
end to end. It publishes nothing.

The [Published image workflow](../.github/workflows/published-image.yml) builds the image that is
downloaded, for amd64 and arm64, on pushes to `main` that touch `internal/image/`, and publishes
it with [`scripts/github-images.sh`](../scripts/github-images.sh) as the `image-<version>` release, which
deletes the previous image release and its tag. GitHub caps an asset at 2 GiB, so the image is split
into parts of 1 GiB that Setup joins.

# Browser cookies

Agents' browsers start signed out. To let them use sites you're signed in to (a staging app, a
dashboard, GitHub), import cookies you export from your own browser into a project: the agents
created afterwards start their Chromium with them.

AgentBox never reads your browser's files. You make the export, you pick the sites.

## Importing

1. Export your cookies with an extension: **Get cookies.txt LOCALLY** (Netscape `cookies.txt`), or
   **Cookie-Editor** / **EditThisCookie** (JSON). A Playwright `storageState` file works too.
2. In the app, open the project's **Settings → Secrets**, and under **Browser cookies** choose
   **Import cookies…**. Paste the export or choose the file.
3. Tick the sites agents should be signed in to, or type domains (`github.com` covers its
   subdomains), and import.

From the command line:

```bash
agentbox browser-cookies import pawly cookies.txt                       # lists the sites in it
agentbox browser-cookies import pawly cookies.txt --domain github.com   # imports those
agentbox browser-cookies status pawly
agentbox browser-cookies remove pawly
```

## What happens to them

- Only the cookies of the domains you picked are kept, sealed like a project secret. No page or
  command shows a cookie again: only the domains and how many.
- An agent created after the import gets them in its Chromium the first time its browser starts.
  Agents created before don't. They aren't environment variables, and agents aren't told their values.
- Importing again replaces the cookies; **Remove** forgets them. Agents that already have them keep
  them until they're destroyed.
- Expired cookies are dropped at import. When a site signs the agents out, export and import again.

Anyone who can use the project's agents is signed in as you on those sites: import what an agent
needs, not your whole browser.

# Building, testing and releasing

[← back to the index](README.md)

## Build and test

```bash
go test ./...
go build -o bin/agentbox ./cmd/agentbox   # reports "agentbox version dev"
npm --prefix desktop run dist             # bin/agentbox with the version in desktop/package.json,
                                           # plus the AppImage, .deb and .pacman in desktop/dist/
```

`bin/` is gitignored, so rebuild it after pulling. `npm --prefix desktop run dist`
(`desktop/scripts/dist.mjs`) builds the Go binary with the version injected via `ldflags`,
compiles the app (`npm run build`), and calls `electron-builder --linux AppImage deb pacman` to
package both together.

## CI

[`.github/workflows/ci.yml`](../.github/workflows/ci.yml) runs on every push to `main` and every
pull request:

- `go vet ./...`, and `go vet -tags integration ./...` — vetting the Incus-dependent tests
  without running them, since CI's runner can't run Incus itself;
- `go test ./...`;
- the desktop app's `npm run typecheck` and `npm run build` (with
  `ELECTRON_SKIP_BINARY_DOWNLOAD=1`, so it doesn't need to fetch Electron's binary just to
  type-check and bundle).

It doesn't package the AppImage — that takes minutes and belongs to a release — and it can't run
the `integration`-tagged Incus tests themselves, only vet them.

## Releasing

Releasing means merging a pull request, not running a script.
[release-please](https://github.com/googleapis/release-please) watches every push to `main` and
keeps a single open "release PR" bumping `version` in `desktop/package.json` and
`desktop/package-lock.json`'s two root `version` fields, and rewriting `CHANGELOG.md` from the pull
requests merged since the last release — every PR's title is a changelog line, so title it for a
user reading the changelog.

Merging that PR is the release: the [Release workflow](../.github/workflows/release.yml) tags the
merge commit, opens a draft GitHub release, and builds
`AgentBox-<version>-x86_64.AppImage`, `AgentBox-<version>-amd64.deb`,
`AgentBox-<version>-x64.pacman`, the Windows installer and portable `.exe`, the command-line tool
for Linux, macOS and (as the front end of the Mac's Linux VM) `darwin`, and the Mac app when the
repository has Apple's signing secrets. Only once every build has succeeded does it upload the
assets, write `SHA256SUMS`, and take the release off draft — a failed build leaves it a draft,
visible to collaborators only, until a rerun gets everything green. The whole build takes a few
minutes.

# Chat over ACP

[← back to the index](README.md)

The app's chat drives all three AI tools — Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode — through the same
protocol: [ACP](https://agentclientprotocol.com), the Agent Client Protocol, JSON-RPC 2.0 over an
agent's stdin and stdout, one message per line. The client side lives in
[`internal/acp`](../internal/acp); the chat manager built on top of it is
[`internal/chat`](../internal/chat).

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Chat["internal/chat\n(chat manager)"]
    Conn["acp.Conn\ninternal/acp/conn.go"]
    subgraph tool["Inside the agent's container"]
        direction TB
        ClaudeAdapter["claude-agent-acp\n(npm package)"] --> Claude["Claude Code"]
        CodexAdapter["codex-acp\n(npm package)"] --> Codex["Codex"]
        OpenCodeBin["opencode acp"] --> OpenCode["OpenCode"]
    end
    Chat --> Conn
    Conn -- "JSON-RPC 2.0, stdio" --> ClaudeAdapter
    Conn -- "JSON-RPC 2.0, stdio" --> CodexAdapter
    Conn -- "JSON-RPC 2.0, stdio" --> OpenCodeBin
```

## ACP client

`internal/acp/conn.go` defines `Conn`, which manages one bidirectional connection to an agent
process: `Call()` sends a request and waits for its response, and a `Handler` interface
(`Notify()`/`Request()`) receives what the agent sends back unprompted — streamed message chunks,
tool-call updates, permission requests, usage updates. `internal/acp/types.go` defines the
protocol's own types: `InitializeRequest`/`Response`, `NewSessionRequest`, `SessionResponse`,
`ConfigOption` (the settings — model, effort, permissions — a client can show the user),
`McpServer` (the MCP servers a session should run, stdio-based) and the usage types `Cost` and
`RateLimit` that feed [the token ledger](tokens.md).

## One adapter per tool

`ChatAdapters`, in [`internal/agent/chat.go`](../internal/agent/chat.go), maps each AI tool to the
binary that speaks ACP for it:

```go
var ChatAdapters = map[string]ChatAdapter{
    "claude":   {Tool: "Claude Code", Command: "claude-agent-acp", Package: image.Pin("npm:@agentclientprotocol/claude-agent-acp")},
    "codex":    {Tool: "Codex", Command: "codex-acp", Package: image.Pin("npm:@agentclientprotocol/codex-acp")},
    "opencode": {Tool: "OpenCode", Command: "opencode", Args: []string{"acp"}, Package: image.Pin("opencode")},
}
```

The versions are the ones the base image pins, in
[`internal/image/tools.txt`](../internal/image/tools.txt).

OpenCode has two releases and an installation chooses between them
(`state.SettingOpenCodeVersion`, `internal/opencode/version.go`). OpenCode 1 is the `opencode`
the tools pin. OpenCode 2 is not part of the image: it is installed on demand, beside it, as `opencode2`, because both
releases carry a command called `opencode`; `openCodeAdapter` swaps the command and drops the
mise package for 2, which runs by name. The ACP side is the same `acp` subcommand in both.

Claude Code and Codex don't speak ACP themselves, so AgentBox runs a separate adapter package in
front of each (`claude-agent-acp`, `codex-acp`) that wraps the tool's own protocol in ACP. OpenCode
speaks ACP natively through its own `acp` subcommand, so there's no wrapper — the adapter is just
`opencode acp`. All three are installed with `mise install` and launched with `mise exec` inside
the agent's container, except OpenCode 2, which each agent installs from its npm package at its first OpenCode 2 start
(`ensureOpenCode2InAgent`) and links into its `~/.local/bin`.

## The chat manager

[`internal/chat/chat.go`](../internal/chat/chat.go) holds one `conversation` per agent (including
the lead), each guarded by its own mutex. A `ChatSession` (`internal/api`) carries the session's
state, which AI tool it is, its `ConfigOption`s, and available slash commands; a `ChatItem`
represents one piece of the transcript — a message, a tool call, a thought, or a subagent card —
each tagged with a kind, its turn, and (for something nested under a subagent) a parent id.
Streamed text is batched before it reaches listeners (a `flushDelay`, around 50ms) rather than
flushed on every token.

A subagent spawned mid-turn (Claude Code's Task tool, for example) is announced by the adapter
with a `subagent_spawned` ACP notification and represented as its own `ChatItem` of kind
`"subagent"`; whatever it says nests underneath by `Parent`, so the transcript reads as a tree
rather than a flat log (`internal/chat/subagents.go`).

## Background work

Claude Code can leave work running after its turn ends: a command run in the background, a
Monitor, a subagent. While any runs the agent shows as **Awaiting**, and the session wakes by
itself when one finishes. The end of the chat lists each one as a chip with its status (running,
done, failed, timed out, stopped). Click a chip to see its command, when it started and ended, its
exit code, and its output, which follows the command live and loads earlier output on request; a
subagent's chip goes to its card in the conversation instead. Ended work stays listed until the
session's AI tool restarts.

What is shown is what the tool's adapter reports (`internal/chat/background.go`):

| | Claude Code | Codex | OpenCode, Cursor, Gemini CLI, Copilot CLI |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Background commands | status, exit code, output read from the command's output file | status, and the output its tool call kept | not reported |
| Monitors | status and summary, no output | n/a | n/a |
| Subagents that outlive their turn | status, with a jump to the card | status, with a jump to the card | not reported |

The same list is `backgroundTasks` on `GET …/chat`, and `GET …/chat/background/{task}` returns one
task with the end of its output (`?before=<offset>` for the piece before).

## The token ledger

[`internal/chat/tokens.go`](../internal/chat/tokens.go)'s `book()` runs once a turn ends: it reads
the turn's per-model token counts from the adapter's `acp.PromptResponse.ByModel`, takes the
turn's cost from a running total the adapter's `usage_update` notifications have been adding to
since the last booking (reset on `/clear`), and writes one row per model via `tokenRows()`
straight to `state.AddTokenRows` — off the chat's own lock, in a background goroutine, so booking
never blocks the conversation. See [The token ledger and Claude accounts](tokens.md) for the
table shape and how it's read back.

## Compaction

A Claude Code chat compacts once its session nears the installation's compact window — 500,000
tokens by default (`DefaultClaudeCompactWindow`, `internal/state/settings.go`), because every model
call resends the whole conversation. A project's `rollover_threshold` (`state.go`, default 80%)
sets how full a session gets, measured against `context_tokens` on the ledger, before AgentBox
rolls it over into a fresh session rather than letting the tool's own compaction kick in.

# Connectors: remote MCP servers for agents

[← back to the index](README.md)

A **connector** is a remote MCP server — Notion, Linear, Sentry, anything that speaks MCP's
streamable HTTP transport — that a project's agents, and its chat, get as tools. You sign in once,
in your own browser; AgentBox keeps the sign-in and adds it to every request an agent makes to the
server. **No token is ever written into an agent's machine**, and an agent never sees one.

## Adding one

In the app, open a project's **Settings** tab, then **Connectors**, and pick Notion, Linear, Sentry
or Figma, or give the address of any other server. Connecting opens your browser at the server's sign-in page; once
you approve AgentBox there, the browser comes back to `http://127.0.0.1:7777/connectors/callback`
and the connector shows as connected. That address is on your own machine, and it reaches AgentBox
wherever AgentBox runs, its VM included, the same way agents' previews do.

From the command line:

```bash
agentbox connector add pawly notion --url https://mcp.notion.com/mcp
agentbox connector connect pawly notion          # opens the browser, waits for the sign-in
agentbox connector list pawly
agentbox connector add pawly figma --url https://mcp.figma.com/mcp --secret FIGMA_TOKEN --header X-Figma-Token
agentbox connector disconnect pawly notion       # forgets the sign-in, keeps the connector
agentbox connector remove pawly/agent-01 linear
```

A connector's address must be `https`, on a server elsewhere: AgentBox refuses one on your own
machine, since agents' requests would go there.

## Who gets it

A connector belongs to a project, and every agent of it gets it, or to one agent. An agent's own
connector of the same name replaces its project's for that agent, the way an agent's own secret
does. The project's chat gets the project's connectors too.

When the chat creates an agent it can give it only some of the project's connectors, or none.

## How it signs in

- **Browser sign-in** (OAuth), the default, for servers that let AgentBox register itself with them:
  Notion, Linear and Sentry do. AgentBox renews the sign-in before it runs out; if the server stops
  accepting it, the connector says "needs connecting again".
- **A token you paste**, kept as one of the project's secrets (`agentbox secrets`) and sent in a
  header, for a server that won't let AgentBox register: Figma is one, and takes a personal access
  token in `X-Figma-Token`.
- **Nothing**, for a public server.

## When an agent asks for one

An agent that needs a service it has no tools for can ask you for it. The request shows as a card in
the chat and at the top of the project's Settings → Connectors, with the server's address: **check that address**,
since the agent chose it. A preset's name, like Notion, only shows when the address is that
service's own. Adding and signing in from the card gives the agent the connector; you can refuse it
instead.

An AI tool reads its MCP servers when its session starts, so a connector connected while an agent
works reaches its tools with its next session. Until then the agent can use it from its shell
(`agentbox connector tools notion`, `agentbox connector call notion …`).

## What it can't do yet

- A session already running keeps the MCP servers it started with: a connector added, removed or
  turned off reaches an agent's AI tool at its next session (Claude Code's `/mcp` reconnects).
- A server that refuses to let AgentBox register, but would take a client ID registered by hand,
  has no way to be given one.
- Figma's remote server wasn't checked with a real personal access token.
- If something else on your machine already listens on port 7777, the browser sign-in can't come
  back to AgentBox: use a token connector, or free the port.

# Diagnostics

[← back to the index](README.md)

When AgentBox feels slow, the daemon can say where the time went. It keeps a trace of its own work
on your machine, and nothing in it is sent anywhere.

## What is kept

- **Spans**: one line for each API request, job, Incus call, git command, AI tool turn (ACP) and
  SQLite transaction the daemon ran, plus the spans the desktop app sends. Each line has its name,
  when it started, how long it took, whether it failed, and a few details. The file is
  `spans.ndjson`, next to `state.db` in AgentBox's data folder (`~/.local/share/agentbox` on
  Linux, inside the VM). It's rotated at 8 MiB, and three older files are kept (`spans.ndjson.1`
  is the newest). On a busy machine that's a few hours.
- **Stalls**: the spans where something was stuck, also written to `stalls.ndjson` (512 KiB and one
  older file, which is days or weeks):
  - the daemon took more than 2 seconds to start answering a request from the app, or it hasn't
    answered after 30 seconds;
  - a SQLite transaction waited more than 1 second for the database's write lock;
  - the VM's memory was stalling (pressure stall information: some task waiting for memory 20% of
    the last 10 seconds, or every task 5%), or its CPU (some task waiting for a CPU 60% of the
    time). One stall covers the whole episode, with the worst it got.
- **Resources**: what the VM and each agent used (CPU, memory, processes, disk), sampled every
  30 seconds and kept in the daemon's memory for an hour.

## `agentbox trace summary`

```bash
agentbox trace summary                         # the last 30 minutes
agentbox trace summary --since 2h --limit 40
```

It reads the files directly, so it works while the daemon is hung or stopped. Each line is one kind
of span: how many ended in the window, how many per minute, how many failed, and the median (P50),
95th percentile (P95), longest (MAX) and total time. The busiest come first, by total time. The
stalls in the window are listed below the table.

Long-lived requests, like the app's event stream or a terminal, count for as long as they stay
open, so they can top the table without being slow.

## The daemon's memory

```bash
agentbox debug heap                            # saves agentbox-heap-<time>.pb.gz here
go tool pprof -top -sample_index=inuse_space agentbox-heap-*.pb.gz
```

`agentbox debug heap` saves what the daemon's heap holds, by where it was allocated, after a garbage
collection, and prints how much is live and how much the daemon has from the system. Go's other
profiles (goroutines, CPU, allocations) are at `/debug/pprof/` on the daemon's socket, and only
there: not to phones or the hub.

The daemon keeps its heap under a soft limit of 256 MiB: near it, Go collects garbage more often
rather than asking for more memory. Set `GOMEMLIMIT` in the daemon's environment to choose another
(`GOMEMLIMIT=512MiB`), or `GOMEMLIMIT=off` for none.

## GitHub's rate limit

GitHub gives each account 5,000 REST requests an hour, and AgentBox's token is shared: the daemon,
the app's views behind it and every agent's own `gh` spend the same budget. `agentbox github usage`
shows what the daemon sent since it started, by account, by what asked (the pull request list, the
pull request watch, the pull request view, issue pickup…) and by endpoint, with what GitHub last said
is left. Its "others" figure is what GitHub counted beyond AgentBox's own requests: mostly agents'
`gh`, and anything else of yours using the token.

AgentBox asks GitHub again for what it already read with its ETag (an unchanged answer is free),
shares a read in flight, reads every open pull request's checks in one GraphQL query, and re-reads
less often once a fifth of the budget is left. Below 5%, its background reads wait for the reset;
once GitHub says the budget is spent, nothing is sent until then, and the app says when that is.
`AGENTBOX_GITHUB_DEBUG=1` in the daemon's environment logs every request.

## The API

The app's Diagnostics page reads the same data over the daemon's socket:

| Route | What it answers |
| --- | --- |
| `GET /v1/diagnostics/spans?since=30m` | per span name: count, errors, p50/p95/max ms; the 50 slowest spans; the latest 50 failures |
| `GET /v1/diagnostics/stalls?since=24h` | the stalls, newest first |
| `GET /v1/diagnostics/resources?window=1h` | the VM's samples and each agent's |
| `POST /v1/diagnostics/client-spans` | the app's own spans, up to 500 at a time, stored with `source: "app"` |
| `GET /v1/github/usage` | each GitHub token's requests since the daemon started, and what is left of its budgets |

# Export and import

Export writes an AgentBox's data into one file; import merges that file into another AgentBox, on
another computer or after a reinstall. The same file works from the CLI and from the app's
**Settings → Export / Import**.

## What goes in the file

Each project's data comes in kinds, each of which you can leave out:

| Kind | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `repository` | The remote URL and branch, or, with `--bundle`, a git bundle of every branch |
| `settings` | The project's settings: accounts, autonomy, models, branch prefix and the rest |
| `sections` | The sidebar section it's in |
| `icon` | Its icon |
| `notes` | Its notes |
| `skills` | The skills switched on for it, and those on for every project |
| `schedules` | Its schedules |
| `memory` | Memories, events, agents' reports and token usage |
| `chats` | The lead's chat and every past agent's (often the largest part) |
| `connectors` | Its connectors and AgentBox-wide ones, as a list: each is signed in to again |
| `secrets` | Its secrets, only when asked for |

Logins are only exported when asked for, each on its own: GitHub accounts, and the Claude Code,
Codex, OpenCode, Cursor, Gemini CLI and GitHub Copilot CLI accounts AgentBox keeps.

Machines, images and worktrees are never in it: the other AgentBox makes them again. Uncommitted
changes in a repository aren't either, bundled or not.

## Encryption

The file is encrypted with a passphrase you type (age's scrypt mode). Without the passphrase it
can't be opened, so keep it. `--no-encrypt` writes it in the clear, which is refused when it holds
secrets or logins.

## From the CLI

```bash
agentbox export --preview                       # what would go in, and how big
agentbox export ~/agentbox.agentbox             # everything but secrets and logins
agentbox export out.agentbox --bundle --secrets --login github,claude
agentbox export out.agentbox --project web --exclude chats,api:memory

agentbox import ~/agentbox.agentbox --dry-run   # what it holds, and what importing would do
agentbox import ~/agentbox.agentbox --repo web=/srv/src/web --exclude claude
```

`--exclude` takes a kind (`memory`), one project's kind (`web:chats`) or, on import, a login
(`github`). The passphrase is asked for, or read from `AGENTBOX_EXPORT_PASSPHRASE`.

## How an import merges

What is already here is skipped, so importing the same file twice changes nothing the second time.
What is here under the same name with other values is a conflict, and this AgentBox's own is kept.
The report lists, for each part, what was added, skipped and conflicted; it's saved under
`~/.local/share/agentbox/imports/`.

A project that isn't here yet needs its repository. Import looks where it was on the other
computer, or where you point it (`--repo name=/path`, or the path field in the app): a checkout
already there is used; otherwise the bundle is restored there when the file has one, else the
remote is cloned there. A project that is here already keeps its repository where it is.

An export from a newer AgentBox than this one is refused: update AgentBox, then import it.

# A hub: your environments in one place

A hub puts every machine running AgentBox in one place — a VPS, another PC, the one you're on — so
the app, the CLI and a browser reach any of them from anywhere. Each machine, an **environment**,
connects out to the hub, so nothing on it has to be reachable. The hub is optional, and a separate
program: `agentbox-hub`.

Nothing on a hub has a password. Whoever opens its **setup link** first becomes its owner, and from
then on everything that connects — the app on another computer, a phone, a browser, an environment —
asks, shows a short code, and is let in once a device already connected **approves** it.

## Run one

```bash
npx agentbox-hub
```

With no flags it keeps its data in SQLite in AgentBox's data directory
(`~/.local/share/agentbox/hub.db`), listens on `127.0.0.1:8080`, and the first time it starts
prints a setup link and its QR code:

```
This hub has no owner yet. Whoever opens this link first becomes its owner:

  http://localhost:8080/hub/setup#abx_l_…
```

Open it in a browser, or paste it into the app's **Connect to a hub…**: you're the owner, and that
browser or app is your first device. The link works once; lost it before using it?
`npx agentbox-hub link` prints another and makes the old one stop working. Once the hub has an owner,
`agentbox-hub link` prints a link that signs the owner in once, within 15 minutes: the way back in
when every device you had is gone.

To reach it from other machines:

- **On your network**: `npx agentbox-hub --listen 0.0.0.0:8080`. The link it prints uses this
  machine's LAN address.
- **On a server**: keep it on `127.0.0.1`, put a TLS proxy such as Caddy in front of it, and give it
  its public address, which goes in the links it makes: `--url https://hub.example.com` (or
  `AGENTBOX_HUB_URL`). `--db postgres://…` keeps its data in Postgres instead.

`npx agentbox-hub --help` lists the rest. `agentbox-hub` is also a single binary, for a service
manager: the npm package only fetches the one for your platform.

## Connect the app

In the app, open the environment menu (top of the sidebar) and choose **Connect to a hub…**:

- Paste the hub's **setup link**, and you're connected as its owner.
- Or type its **address** (`https://hub.example.com`). The app shows a code like `BCDF-GHJK` and its
  QR code, and opens the hub's approval page in your browser. Approve it there (a browser that's
  connected to the hub), scan the QR code with a phone that is, or type the code into the app on a
  computer that is (**Approve a device…**). The app connects as soon as it's approved.

The CLI does the same: `agentbox login https://hub.example.com` prints the code, the approval link
and the QR code, and waits; `agentbox login <setup link>` uses the link. Then `agentbox env list`,
and `--env <name>` on any command.

## Connect an environment

On the machine you want to reach, open its AgentBox app, and in the environment menu, under the hub,
choose **Connect this AgentBox to the hub**. That's it: its AgentBox asks the hub, the app approves
the request itself since it's connected to the hub, and the machine connects, as an environment
named after its hostname. It reconnects by itself, also after restarts.

A machine without the app, like a VPS:

```bash
agentbox remote connect https://hub.example.com
```

It prints a code, the approval link and its QR code, and connects once you approve it from any
connected device. `agentbox remote status` says how it's doing, `agentbox remote disconnect` leaves.

## Approve, list and revoke devices

- **Approve a device…** (in the app, under the hub) takes the code a phone, a computer or a machine
  shows, says what it is and where it's asking from, and approves or denies it. Approve only what
  you started yourself, just now: an approved device can use every environment on the hub. Codes
  last 10 minutes.
- **Devices…** lists what's connected, and when each was last used; **Revoke** signs one out for
  good. It can ask again, and needs approving again.
- In a browser, the hub's own page (`https://hub.example.com/hub/`) does both, and lists the
  environments. A browser that isn't connected yet connects at `/hub/connect`.

An unused device signs out after 90 days.

## Accounts from before

Hubs used to have accounts with an email and a password (`agentbox-hub user add`). Those keep
working: the oldest one is the hub's owner, and approves devices like any other; their sessions
show up in **Devices…**; and they can still sign in with their password — the app's **Use a
password instead**, `agentbox login <hub> --email you@example.com`, or the hub's page — so nobody is
locked out by updating the hub. `agentbox-hub user password` still resets one. New accounts aren't
made with a password any more, and `--open-signup` does nothing.

## Phones

An environment's phones pair with it directly, not through the hub: see [Chatting from your phone](phone.md). A
hub with a Cloudflare zone gives each environment a stable address for them, on the internet. A hub
on Tailscale puts each environment in your tailnet instead, where only your own devices reach it.

## Other apps

An assistant such as Claude, ChatGPT or Poke can use an environment over remote MCP, at the hub's
`/mcp`: see [Using AgentBox from another app](other-apps.md). The environment's owner pairs each app
on the machine itself, and the hub only relays.

## Tailscale instead of Cloudflare

```bash
AGENTBOX_HUB_TAILSCALE_AUTHKEY=tskey-auth-… npx agentbox-hub --transport tailscale --tailscale-tailnet example.com
```

With `--transport tailscale` (or `AGENTBOX_HUB_TRANSPORT=tailscale`), each environment that asks
for its phones' address gets a key into your [tailnet](https://tailscale.com/kb/1136/tailnet)
instead of a Cloudflare Tunnel. Its AgentBox joins the tailnet as a machine of its own, named
`agentbox-<name>-<id>`, serves its phone page there with `tailscale serve`, and tells the hub its
address, like `https://agentbox-vps-3fa9c0.tail1234.ts.net/`. Nothing is on the internet: only
devices signed in to your tailnet reach it, and the hub sees none of that traffic. Pairing works
exactly as with Cloudflare: a QR code from the environment, which the hub can't make.

The environment runs Tailscale itself, downloaded the first time (checked against its published
checksum), in userspace mode, next to AgentBox: it needs no root, adds no network interface, and
leaves a Tailscale you run yourself on that machine alone. A device not on the tailnet can't open
the address; the phone app says so and asks you to turn Tailscale on.

### Set up the tailnet

In Tailscale's admin console:

1. **DNS**: turn on **MagicDNS** and **HTTPS Certificates**. The environment's address is its
   MagicDNS name, with a certificate from Let's Encrypt; that name is published in public
   certificate logs, like any certificate's.
2. **Access controls**: add a tag for environments, and let your devices reach it on port 443:

   ```json
   {
     "tagOwners": {
       "tag:agentbox": ["autogroup:admin"]
     },
     "grants": [
       { "src": ["autogroup:member"], "dst": ["tag:agentbox"], "ip": ["tcp:443"] }
     ]
   }
   ```

   Merge these into the policy you have. With only this grant, environments can't reach your
   devices or each other. A tailnet still on the default allow-all policy lets everything through;
   the tag is needed either way.

3. Give the hub a way to add environments, one of:
   - **An auth key** (Settings → Keys → Generate auth key): **Reusable**, **Pre-approved**, and
     **Tags** `tag:agentbox`. Put it in `AGENTBOX_HUB_TAILSCALE_AUTHKEY`, or in a file named by
     `AGENTBOX_HUB_TAILSCALE_AUTHKEY_FILE`. Every environment gets this key. Keys expire (90 days
     at most): when it does, make another and restart the hub. Environments already in the tailnet
     stay, since a tagged machine's own key doesn't expire.
   - **An OAuth client** (Settings → OAuth clients): scopes **Auth Keys** (write) and **Devices →
     Core** (write), with the tag `tag:agentbox`. Give the hub its ID, `--tailscale-oauth-client`
     or `AGENTBOX_HUB_TAILSCALE_OAUTH_CLIENT`, and its secret in
     `AGENTBOX_HUB_TAILSCALE_OAUTH_SECRET` (or `…_SECRET_FILE`). The hub makes each environment a
     key of its own that works once, within an hour, and removes an environment's machine from the
     tailnet when you delete the environment, or after 60 days unseen.

Keys and secrets are read from the environment or a file, never from a flag, and never logged.
`--tailscale-tailnet` (or `AGENTBOX_HUB_TAILSCALE_TAILNET`) is the tailnet's name from Settings →
General, `-` (the key's own) by default. `--tailscale-tag` uses another tag than `tag:agentbox`.

### On your devices

Install Tailscale on the phone (or the other computer) and sign in to the same tailnet. Pair as
usual: **Settings → Phone** on the environment shows the tailnet address in its QR code.

A hub moved from Cloudflare to Tailscale replaces each environment's tunnel the next time it asks,
and removes the old tunnel from Cloudflare if you leave it its zone and token. Moved back, it makes
them tunnels again. Phones pair again after either move: the address changed.

# Installing AgentBox

AgentBox is a desktop app with the `agentbox` command-line tool inside. One command checks your
computer and installs it. On Linux and on a Mac:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://downloads.agentbox.linting.dev/install.sh | sh
```

On Windows, in PowerShell:

```powershell
irm https://downloads.agentbox.linting.dev/install.ps1 | iex
```

Then open **AgentBox** (on a Mac and on Windows it opens by itself). Its **Setup** does the rest
the first time it runs: it makes AgentBox's VM, or on Windows its WSL distro, installing WSL first
when it's missing; gets the machine your agents are copied from; and logs you in to Claude Code,
Codex or OpenCode.

(See [macOS and Windows](#macos-and-windows-alpha) for what those two are and aren't yet.)

## What the install script does

Before it downloads anything, it checks that this computer can run AgentBox, and lists everything
that's missing at once, in plain words. On Linux:

| Check | Needs | If it's missing |
|---|---|---|
| Processor | x86_64 (Linux on ARM isn't supported yet) | It stops. |
| Virtualization | `/dev/kvm`, for AgentBox's VM | No virtualization: it stops, and says to turn on Intel VT-x or AMD-V in the firmware's settings, or nested virtualization in a VM. A `/dev/kvm` you can't open yet, or KVM's module not loaded, is fine: Setup fixes both (see [below](#kvm)). |
| Memory | 8 GB | It stops. |
| Disk | 30 GB free in your home folder, where the VM's disk goes | It stops. |
| FUSE | `/dev/fuse` and libfuse2, only for the AppImage | It stops, and names the package to install. |

Then it downloads the latest release, checks it against the release's `SHA256SUMS`, and installs
the package that fits your distribution:

- **Debian and Ubuntu**: the `.deb`, with `apt-get` (asks for your password, through `sudo`).
- **Arch** and its derivatives: the `.pacman`, with `pacman` (asks for your password, through `sudo`).
- **Anything else**, Fedora included: the AppImage, in `~/.local/bin/AgentBox.AppImage`, with an
  entry in your applications menu. No password.

**On a Mac** it checks for macOS 13 or later, 8 GB of memory and 30 GB free, then downloads the
`.zip` for your Mac (Apple silicon or Intel), checks it, and puts **AgentBox** in `/Applications`
(or `~/Applications` when that one isn't yours to write to), replacing a copy that's there, and
opens it. No password. A download made by `curl` isn't quarantined, so the app opens without the
right-click **Open** a browser's download needs while the app isn't notarized. Quit AgentBox first
when it's open: the script stops and says so.

**On Windows**, `install.ps1` checks for 64-bit Windows 10 version 2004 or later (or Windows 11),
8 GB of memory and 30 GB free on the drive with `%LOCALAPPDATA%`, where AgentBox keeps its WSL

| `-NoOpen` | `$env:AGENTBOX_INSTALL_NO_OPEN = 1` | Don't open AgentBox afterwards |

| Option | What |

| `--check` | Only the checks: says what it would install, downloads nothing |
